speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak to Bill C-69. First of all, however, I would like to congratulate the Prime Minister of Canada on his concluding, for the second time, an agreement that is historic both for Quebec and the rest of the country. I also would like to emphasize the work done by the ten Premiers, and I think that is appropriate considering the subject of Bill C-69 which deals with transfers to the provinces.
Government Orders
Madam Speaker, Bill C-69 has various objectives and follows announcements by the Minister of Finance and the President of the Treasury Board, with respect to cutbacks in government spending. There will be cuts totalling $3 billion in 1990-91, and $3.8 billion in 1991-92, all of which will cut directly into government spending. This means we have a projected deficit of $28.5 billion for 1990-91 and $26.8 billion for 1991-92.
Madam Speaker, since 1984, this government has started managing the country the way it should be managed, by reducing the annual deficit, which was enormous, and at the same time gradually getting the national debt under control, a debt that was a legacy from the previous government.
So there have been cuts, madam Speaker, including cuts in transfers to the provinces. However, we should be careful when we talk about transfers to the provinces, because often people tend to confuse Established Programs Financing with equalization. Quebec, for instance, receives under Established Programs Financing, certain amounts of money, like all the other provinces. As you know, all provinces receive the same amount per capita under this program.
Furthermore, Madam Speaker, as you know, equalization payments are only paid to certain provinces. These are amounts of money for provinces who are considered the most in need. And Quebec is one of those provinces.
If we look at the figures for 1989-90, the province of Quebec will receive $9.9 billion. In 1990-91, this will be $10.3 billion, and in 1991-92, $10.6 billion. Madam Speaker, this means an increase of about 3 per cent per year. I agree the increase is not as high as the province or other provinces might have expected. However, as a result of Draconian measures we had to take to control the government's annual deficit and the growing national debt, we had to announce a number of reductions in annual increases received by the provinces.
Bill C-69 confirms that the provinces will receive more money next year than they are getting this year, and it also confirms federal participation in helping the provinces.
Madam Speaker, I may point out that since 1977, the provinces have the right to spend the money they receive from the federal government at their own discretion.

June 11, 1990
Government Orders
This means, and I am taking Quebec as an example, if the province receives $10.3 billion in 1990-91, it can invest that money in hospitals, schools, highways, daycare-whatever. That is its personal decision as a province. British Columbia can do the same, and Newfoundland as well. These are sums of money that are allocated in terms of the needs and expectations of each province, but itis strictly discretionary spending.
Madam Speaker, I believe this bill should be passed as soon as possible so that we can get on with our legislative and economic agenda.

Madam Speaker, one thing has become tragically clear as this government's mandate unfolds. Put simply, the Minister of National Health and Welfare has surrendered, without a fight, his responsibility for social policy in this country. It is clear that it is the Minister of Finance who now makes social policy for this government.
What is the result of this abdication of responsibility by the Minister of National Health and Welfare? It is Bill C-21, which will punish the unemployed for this government's failure to come up with a full employment policy. It is Bill C-28, which ends the universality of old age pension and family allowance. It is Bill C-69, which saddles the poor of this country with a disproportionate share of the national debt and which threatens the future viability of our health care system and our post-secondary institutions.
This process, most aptly described as social policy by stealth, has resulted in the polarization of Canadians. The facts are that what we are witnessing is a drastic decline in the numbers who can be considered in the middle class in this country. We are seeing more poor and more rich, with the disappearance of those in the middle; more highly paid jobs and more poorly paid jobs; more children and single parents living in deep poverty; and more people with only a part-time or marginal attachment to the workforce.
This bill, which the government is ramming through, is illustrative of the re-emergence of the Conservative belief in an ordered society, a society of haves and have-nots, a society of rich and poor. It is a rejection of
the concept of collective entitlement and an embracing of paternalism.
The government asks that we all share in the strong medicine needed to control the deficit, but its actions betray its words. This government does not spread the burden equitably but punishes and overburdens those least able to cope.
In this House, as reported at page 10673 of Hansard, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance stated:
The effort that we are requiring from the population with the cuts and the tax hikes is a collective effort on the part of all Canadians. We are asking eveiyone of them, whatever the province they live in, to share in this collective effort-
However, is this the case, Madam Speaker? Is everyone being asked to share? Of course not?
Bill C-69 is a direct attack on the income support of poor Canadians. It is a direct attack on those who are least able to put food on the table, to clothe and house their children, to find meaningful employment. This government has not gone after the incomes of the wealthy. It has not even sought out the deferred taxes of profitable corporations. It has sought out the powerless and gone after them.
As reported at page 10672 of Hansard, the parliamentary secretary also had the following to say about the ceiling placed on Canada Assistance Plan payments by this bill:
The expenditure control plan will not affect the amount received by low income Canadian men and women.
Where in this bill are we to find this? Are we simply to take the word of the parliamentary secretary? 6 the purpose of this bill is to control expenditure, how can he say that it will not affect the amount received by poor Canadians?
The stated purpose of this bill is to force the provinces to absorb a greater share of the national debt. How, one must ask, are they to do that if they do not cut expenditures? How can the parliamentary secretary claim that no one will suffer a loss in income if the provinces are forced to cut income support payments because of the federal government's reneging on its constitutional and contractual responsibility to cost share these expenditures?
June 11, 1990

It is evident to all who care to look that to live on social assistance is to live in poverty. Absolutely nowhere in this country are social assistance rates above the poverty line, no matter which poverty line is used.
The shallowness of understanding demonstrated by members opposite is even more clear when one reads the words of the chair of the finance committee, as reported at page 10551 of Hansard, who had the following to say about Bill C-69:
This bill is a sensible bill because it comes to grips with the EPF, the
CAP, the growth of expenditures and the transfers made from the
federal government to the provinces.
No reference is made to the abandonment of the poor, the abandonment of universality, the abandonment of the social safety net.
The difficulty with the observation of the chair of the finance committee is that it ignores the facts. The Canada Assistance Plan is not a transfer to the provinces; it is a transfer to individuals. The federal government writes the cheque to the province, but what it is paying for is previously agreed upon services and income support payments to those Canadians who are in dire need of this support.
To claim that the cap on CAP is an attempt to control transfers to provinces is to indulge in a purposeful misunderstanding of the Canada Assistance Plan and how it is used by the provinces.
The chairman of the finance committee went on to say on the same page that:
We cannot pay our bills by encouraging profligacy in the hands of
the provinces.
Profligacy means recklessly extravagant. Again, I hope through ignorance rather than a deliberate attempt to mislead, the hon. member reflects the dearth of knowledge on the government side of the House.
Payments made under the Canada Assistance Plan are demand led expenditures. They come from the commitment made by the provinces and the federal government to assist individuals in providing the most basic requirements of life for themselves and their families.
These expenditures are the result of the requirements of the act to provide services having as their object the lessening, removal or prevention of the causes and effects of poverty, child neglect or dependence on public
Government Orders
assistance. Is the hon. member, his party, or the minister actually suggesting that the provinces are being recklessly extravagant in their spending in these areas?
Are they suggesting that neglected children should suffer while this government kisses the ring of the knobby finger of corporate Canada? The finance committee heard witnesses representing 20 groups and organizations, many of which are national organizations.
From these groups not one came before the committee to praise Bill C-69. They came to buiy it. It needs to be noted that they often sat before the committee without the benefit of a single Tory member of the committee, save for the chair of that committee.
The absence of Tories from the committee room provided real and tangible evidence of the lack of concern this government has for the poor, for our universities and colleges and for our health care system. It demonstrated in more than a symbolic way the lack of understanding and caring which is becoming the hallmark of this government.
Before the committee, the Minister of State for Finance made much of his government's plan to get its fiscal house in order and that Bill C-69 represented a way to have the provinces share in that responsibility. It has chosen to do so by limiting its constitutional, contractual and moral responsibilities.
The government has chosen to do so despite the overwhelming evidence provided by a series of government-sponsored studies which demonstrate in unequivocal terms that the Canada Assistance Plan works. It is an effective and efficient use of government resources, and any changes to the Canada Assistance Plan should be made in co-operation with the provinces and those responsible for the delivery of the services covered by CAP.
Such changes should not be ad hoc as they are in this bill, but ones that provide for improved service delivery and a real commitment to getting people off welfare. It should not be a kind of punitive, mean-spirited measure that we see in this bill.
The most recently completed study of the Canada Assistance Plan is now in the hands of the minister, and one cannot help but wonder why he is permitting Bill C-69 to go ahead when he knows it will threaten the most basic component of our social safety net, when he knows that no one in this country with any knowledge of

June 11, 1990
Government Orders
CAP supports the imposition of a ceiling on federal expenditures.
This study brought together acknowledged experts on CAP and this is what they had to say: "CAP is something that is really the best we have got right now. If anything, we should look at improving it rather than taking shots at it."
Another said: "CAP has been called the best example of co-operative federalism-.The province's inputs were respected-.and they were committed to a new approach of social assistance which would eliminate all the vestiges of the poor law and make the concept of need really meaningful."
A third quote is: "The impact of CAP has been enormous-for good or for ill, anything that existed before was incredibly punitive-.It was a terrible, terrible system-.The level of brutality was spectacular."
A final quote is: "I would like to state that if anything happens to the CAP agreement and the transfer monies-effect on the provinces in the next five years would be chaotic. It would be one of the most disastrous things Ottawa could ever do."
Those quotes are from references submitted to the Program Audit Review directorate of Health and Welfare Canada by the DPA group incorporated.
I would suggest that it is the desire of the government to return to the brutality that is referred to in those quotes, to see a return to the belief which pervaded the poor laws, a belief which regarded the disadvantaged as at fault for their plight.
If this government was really concerned about saving money it would look to creative and positive ways to alleviate poverty in this country. It would be supportive of the provinces in their attempt to deliver the services low-income Canadians need. It would embrace a policy of full employment. This bill proposes to cut short that creativity and sentence the poor in Canada to further hardship. In short, this bill needs to be defeated.
In closing I would like to make reference to an article in The Globe and Mail of June 7, written by Hovi Echenberg from NAPO:
So, despite the silence of ministers traditionally playing the lead in
social-policy changes, the web of federal policy initiatives has
changed things for the worse for people at the edges of the marketplace. It may be that what used to be a safety net is becoming a trap, or even a noose, for Canada's poor.
In British Columbia, Alberta, and Ontario, the provincial governments will resist real increases in social assistance income levels because, for the first time in more than 20 years, these increases will not be cost shared by the federal government. In these same provinces, the same limit on cost sharing will likely preclude new child care spaces, or increased civil legal aid services to support appeals of any disentitlement.
In every province in Canada, low income people will likely find that few health services are insured under medicare. Whether annual physicals, ambulance services or drugs prescribed during a hospital stay, new costs will be borne by individuals. Affordable housing units will be slower to come by on the market, as federal funding for non-profit housing programs is reduced.
Madam Speaker, my caucus agrees with Hovi Echenberg when she says that the safety net is becoming a trap, or even a noose, for the poor.

Madam Speaker, I listened with a great deal of interest to my colleague from Mission-Coquitlam and I would like to compliment her on a very thoughtful presentation of the arguments. It was very well thought through.
I join her and members of my caucus to speak on Bill C-69, an act respecting restraint of government expenditures. This bill implements four measures for budget restrictions announced in the budget of February 1990. First there is the freeze to federal transfer payments to the provinces for post-secondary education and health care under the Established Program Financing. Second, there is the limit on the increase of federal transfer payments to Ontario, British Columbia, and Alberta under the Canada Assistance Plan, which includes social programs. Third, there is the elimination of the Canada Exploration Incentives Program which affects mining, gas and oil industries. Fourth, is the measure that freezes public utilities income tax transfers over the next two years.
This bill represents, in a sense, the entire lack of balance in this government's approach between what I have always called two important pillars of Canada: economic opportunity and social justice. In my view, the two must be pursued simultaneously for both are critical objectives if we are to have the kind of Canada we have always striven for.
June 11, 1990

To forsake one for the interests of the other is to fail. To blindly fight the deficit without regard for the human and social toll is also to fail as a government and ultimately as a society.
Yet, that is this government's approach, as this bill demonstrates. This government concerns itself solely with the deficit at the expense of all else. While concerning itself with the economic side of the balance, pursuing deficit reduction and what it calls economic stability, it is forgetting how important it is to have social stability and a truly caring society.
There is no question that the people of this country need policies that are fiscally sound. They need to address the deficit. They also need policies that have no regard to class or place but provide for equitable consideration. Only our government can be expected to serve as that dependable link and ensure non-discrimination between the densely populated areas of our country and small-town Canada. Towns and villages should not be preferred over our cities, or prosperous communities to the less fortunate. Equality of service has been a valued Canadian hallmark and it seems to me that it is being eroded on a daily basis. A wonderful safety net is becoming less and less so.
The government has not seen it this way. I believe it has chosen to disrupt, to dismantle and even destroy much of this country's vital infrastructure, conceived to answer our very unique geography. Our huge land mass, with communities of varying sizes dispersed around this vast region, many sparsely settled, all need service. Be it social service, education or health, they have to be shared with our provinces; be it the national mandate on job skills, retraining, communications and transportation, these are all the key elements in the building and linking of our people to ensure a bright future and a sense of national unity.
The government has cut back on the CBC. It says this was needed to fight the deficit, forgetting that it is a bridge for Canadians to bring a national voice to all parts of this land, with the technology and vital infrastructure which brings about an informed Canadian society.
Today, I was pleased to participate in the launching of Digital Radio, La radio numerique, which will fill in the
Government Orders
blanks that you would normally have as you drive from your home to Ottawa when the sound fades and there is interference from American channels. We will have new technology to correct that.
We must not destroy that infrastructure. Without the money that the CBC needs, we will not have the required infrastructure to ensure that we will have the kinds of communication that we require across this land.
What else has the government done? It has tom down VIA Rail because of the deficit. Forget about the social costs and the hardship it causes the elderly, the sick and women who have to take their children from distant locations to Montreal but cannot travel on the buses because it is inconvenient and uncomfortable. It is the same hardship for the disabled and the handicapped who cannot afford air fare. They were forgotten while it dismantled the wonderful transportation net that we had set up. The government would rather forget about the social costs of removing vital links across this land; the deficit is the only thing that matters.
Bill C-69 continues to implement the cuts of the government's 1990 budget. As I mentioned, the CBC capital budget has been cut by $20 million. That would certainly affect radio transmission and, I suggest, cuts very important services to the north. Telefilm Canada was cut by $13 million, affecting our Canadian content for film and video. The Export Development Corporation which helps our companies compete around the world, which is supposed to be another goal of this government, was cut by $100 million. The Secretary of State was cut by $113 million, much of it to womens' support programs and aboriginal communication infrastructure. The Small Craft Harbours Program was cut by $29 million. The Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation funding for social and co-operative housing was cut by $165 million in the face of acute shortages in low-cost housing and a growing homeless population in many of our major cities.
The trickery being played here is obvious. The government makes these cuts while its rhetoric speaks of strong undying support for the varied programs it is cutting. Who are those members they trying to fool? The smoke and mirrors are easy to see through. Canadians have certainly not been duped with these hollow words.

June 11, 1990
Government Orders
After six years, Canadians know all too well how the game is being played on that side of the House: a government claiming support for programs while cutting them; and a government claiming it has performed miracles of fiscal management, when it has doubled the national debt and taken Canadian taxpayers to the cleaners. There have been 31 tax increases, with the thirty-second in the wings.
I am not saying that we must ignore the deficit, not at all. Nor do I believe any of my colleagues believe that-
Sure, they do.

-but we must apply to any deficit action the traditional Canadian approach of balance between the economic and social goals.
I certainly would not use the hon. member's very narrow point of perspective. I remember him on one of my standing committees and it was not a pleasure.
In other words, we must examine the social cost of any given action on the deficit. If we give up on that principle, we give up on what has been one of the fundamental values of Canada. I would argue we would be vastly impaired, not fairly meeting all of our citizens' basic needs. It would pander to the well-to-do and be quite insensitive to the growing needs of the working poor.
With the budget. Bill C-69, and all the other blind cuts that have occurred, the government has failed on this question of social responsibility. I would suggest to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, if he is truly concerned, that his voice has been silenced. He has failed to have an impact on the thinking of his cabinet colleagues. He has failed to have an impact on the budget of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance and he has succeeded only in loosening the web of the Canadian social fabric.
What a strange irony as we open the newspapers today and we see that the Minister of Finance is busy asking workers and unions to limit their wage increase demands. At the same time, the government treats its own public servants quite differently. I would suggest, again, that that fancy rhetoric does not really reflect reality. It is really quite a scandal, what we learned today.
We learned that, while telling workers to cut their wage demands, the Tory government has been quietly topping up the salaries of high level federal executives with bonuses of up to 25 per cent. I told the Minister of Transport that he should change jobs. At the 25 per cent
limit, the estimate is that he would get a bonus of almost $40,000 as the head of VIA Rail and $100,000 as the head of Petro-Can.
I recall in Question Period today the President of the Treasury Board spoke in the most unctuous tones, using holier-than-thou terms. He ended by saying: "Eve told you that the government bosses received exactly the same pay increases as the workers of the country. As unionized public servants, they got a 4.2 per cent increase." He just forgot about the bonuses. It seems to me it just banks all these people bank who certainly got more than 4.2 per cent. There has been a lack of full exposure of this issue.
The salary range for the Bank of Canada Governor, John Crow, has risen by 35 per cent since 1987. We had to get information, not through Canada's access to information legislation, but through the American access to information system. We found out that the five top executives at CN received pay raises averaging 18.7 per cent last year, the same year that CN's profits plunged. Then, two days ago, my colleague, the hon. member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon, came into the House and asked the Minister of Labour what he plans to do for the 1,900 CN workers who just lost their jobs-

I ask you, is that really fair? Personally, I find it really unacceptable.

The cuts we have had to the Canada Assistance Plan, in the provinces of Ontario, British Columbia and Alberta, will increase the strain on the already insufficient resources available, not only for the general welfare services but also for services for the disabled, for child care, for foster homes-the whole range of social services. This is the first time in the 24-year history of the Canada Assistance Plan that the federal government has placed a limit on its contributions. Created in 1966, this legislation provides the basis for social assistance in the country.
By cutting CAP, the federal government is hurting the poorest of the poor. Under CAP, the federal and provincial governments share equally in the cost of welfare payments and basic necessities such as food, shelter, clothing, utilities, and other household supplies. It also provides important services such as dental care for the poor, essential services for disabled persons, foster
June 11, 1990

homes for abused children, shelters for abused wives, and child care for low income families.
The data for 1987 shows that 49 per cent of Canada's poor families and 54 per cent of Canada's poor individuals live in these three provinces. The cuts that the federal government has imposed are unilateral, defying at least the spirit, if not the wording, of the CAP agreement with the provinces. The contesting provinces believe that under the CAP agreement, CAP can only be modified after a year's notice and with provincial consent. This is the government that is building a great sense of national reconciliation and goodwill. I will not comment further right now on that issue.
I would suggest to you that neither of these provisions have been met. Madam Speaker, don't look so upset. The truth is the truth, even if it hurts and makes you unhappy.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: You didn't mention the 5 per cent increase the Ontario government was implementing.

Then what is the freeze that you are putting into place? You forget to take account of that.
The problem with the hon. members opposite is that they are a bunch of penguins. They do not read the documents. All they do is flap their wings and their lips.
Through capping the Canada Assistance Plan, the government claims it will save $151 million over two years. That is what it has done through capping. That is its bottom line. What are the costs? The Canada Council on Social Development has stated:
Poor children will suffer when Ihe federal contribution to the
Canada Assistance Plan is capped for Alberta, B.C. and Ontario.
The plan provides direct payments to poor people with no other
income, 40 per cent of whom are children and half of whom live in
the three provinces that are affected.
The poor in these three provinces are just as poor as those in other provinces and this is a very odd way for the government to come to the aid of those in need.
That is the human toll I am talking about, the cost in human and social terms of this deficit cutting action. Yes, perhaps the provinces will fill in the gap left by the federal government where they have been able to maintain their resolve and their commitment to the caring society. I say, thank goodness someone will,
Government Orders
because it is surely not going to be those on the benches across the way who will act in the interest of our poor, especially our children.
Something is dreadfully wrong in the orientation and planning for our country. Something is wrong with the vision of the government.
While the Minister of Finance is very pleased with his budget, all he has done is transfer the burden of tax to the provinces and the municipalities. By the government's shirking of its duties to make its budget look better, other hands are going into the taxpayers' pockets to meet important needs in terms of assistance, health, re-education, and training.
Let us look at the Equalization Payment Fund and education cuts. What is the impact of the minister's cuts? What is the implication of these freezes, cuts, or whatever you want to call them? It is less money going into the province to support the importance of education and the future of our children.
Will the provinces faced with less than their expected federal contributions have any choice with provincial transfers being strained? Have they any choice but to give further limited resources to the universities? Will they have any choice but to increase tuition or to put capital projects or new equipment purchases on hold? Who suffers then? The student suffers because either tuition increases have closed the door to college or to university, or the institution cannot afford all the resources to prepare him or her for the fierce competition of life and career.
This only serves as a stumbling block in maximizing the potential of our young people who are our human capital of tomorrow. These are the kinds of things the government must be able to see and duly consider-the full consequences of its action and not just the effect on the balance sheet. Unfortunately, Canadians do not have a government with that kind of balanced vision. We do have a government that knows how to package pretty packages, empty boxes, but it does not remember its own strongly held view.
Unfortunately I have misplaced one of the minister's famous quotes, but it indicates that he does not feel we should be cutting on the backs of the hospitals, health care, or the universities when we look at how to plan. He

June 11, 1990
Government Orders
said this in 1982 but I guess when one becomes minister there is another reality that sets in.
These are not the first cuts to education transfers by the government. Cumulatively, since 1986, it has cut $31.1 billion from all EPF programs-$22.2 billion from health care and $8.9 billion from post-secondary education. Across the way, members may not call them a cut nor a freeze but any name they want. It is $31.1 billion: $22.2 billion plus $8.9 billion. Most people do not even know how many zeroes that is. They just know that it is a heck of a lot of money being cut from the needed services for their children and for their future.
This is being done at a time when inflation is running above 5 per cent, heating costs are up, library costs have risen, new equipment is sorely needed, and laboratory costs are on the increase. Again, the government has made the cuts in education transfers to the provinces just when what is really needed are greater resources for education, better facilities, and more professors to make our young people capable of competing in the 21st century.
In an address to a public policy conference for journalists convened by the C. D. Howe Institute in April, 1989, George Pederson, the president of the University of Western Ontario, issued a very severe warning saying that the university system in Canada is in trouble, serious trouble.
I am going to wrap up by saying that it is certain that we have pockets of excellence in our various educational institutions, but there is no single university in Canada that can compete with the best in the United States, Britain, Western Europe, not to mention Japan. If we want to be on a fair and equal footing to compete in the international world of tomorrow, we had better make sure there is a reinstatement of quality in our universities. That is what Pederson maintained and he is quoted in an article in The London Free Press of April 28, 1990.
When one cuts into the health care of the people and the basic promises for the infrastructure of our health services, and when the world looks our medicare system and says that this is an incredible system, this population is no longer prepared to accept the kinds of cuts the government has put in. We find that we are closing beds
and have long waiting lists in our hospitals and overcrowded emergency wards-all things which are taking place as we cut $22.2 billion from the EPF. With respect to our health services, the cutbacks announced are absolutely amazing and 70 per cent of that $31.1 billion comes from that health care side.
Madam Speaker, I would have liked to continue. Another time I will have something else to say.

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I listened with great interest to the hon. member's speech this afternoon. She made three very interesting points. She criticized the government for cutting expenditures; she criticized the government for raising taxes; and she criticized the government for not handling the deficit problems.
There is a certain inconsistency in that type of speech. There are two areas where the federal government can save income or gain income. One is through taxes and the other is through cutting expenditures. If we do have a deficit problem the hon. member will have to admit to the House-at least I hope she would admit to the House-that one, the other or both is a way to try to get the deficit situation under control. That is what the Minister of Finance has done in a very responsible manner.
She talked about the deficit of this country. When we took office, it was $200 billion, it is now some $350 billion, 80 per cent of which is just compound interest on the $200 billion deficit that was left to us.
Why don't you do something about it?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext:
That is exactly what we are doing. The hon. member can stand up and criticize all she wants. That is very easy. The minute the Liberal Party has something concrete to put on the table to solve the
June 11, 1990

deficit problem, we will be very pleased to listen to it, and if it makes sense we will take action.

Madam Speaker, this government has been in place for over six years, six of the best earning years in the history of Canada, and all it has managed to do is double the national debt and not decrease the deficit. Go and find out what you are supposed to do. They didn't elect me to do it. They elected you to do it. Why don't you take your responsibilities seriously. And by the way, why don't you eat crow or fire Crow, but stand behind what you do?

Madam Speaker, I too have a question for the hon. member for Mount Royal. She mentioned during the course of her speech that members on the other side were not able to get their message through to the Minister of Finance. She made that point very well. She also made the point that the hon. member for Jonquiere, the hon. member for Niagara Falls, and the hon. member for St. John's East, and finally the Minister for Privatization did not get their message through to her either, and I hope they never do, because she did a very good job.
The Minister of Finance said in Toronto in August, 1984 that he would not increase taxes in Canada in order to cut the deficit. He has raised them 31 times and is coming up to 32 times. He also said he would not make a battleground out of post-secondary education, hospitalization and medicare in this country, but he has done that very thing in Bill C-69.
While we are talking about inconsistencies, I would like to put this question to the hon. member for Mount Royal. Do you think these are greater inconsistencies than the phoney arguments raised by the Minister for Privatization?

Madam Speaker, I could not have said it better than my colleague, and I thank him for those remarks. I would just like to remind him about one thing the Prime Minister had to say. At the PC general meeting on August 25, 1989, he said: "This government will carry its fair share of the burden to ensure that all young Canadians receive a first-class education as they
Government Orders
confront a world-class challenge". Certainly, the Minister of Finance did not hear that. I would like to remind him of what the Prime Minister had to say and recall his own words for reconsideration so he might withdraw the bill. On March 24, 1982, he said: "Cuts to the EPF could have disastrous effects on the universities and on the colleges, on the hospital funding and on the operation of the hospitals. Madam Speaker, I would like to ask the hon. member for Mount Royal a question, bearing in mind the comment in her speech that Canadian universities are not as high in excellence as those in other countries, such as the United States, England, and others.
First of all, I want to submit that while she may be basing her quote on a newspaper article, I do not think most Canadians or most international observers would agree with her. I would like her to indicate what universities in Canada she believes to be inferior to those international universities. I would think that the foreign students coming to Canada will claim that part of the reason they come here is because our universities stand in their excellence, par excellence, second to none. I ask her if she has any empirical evidence to support that unsubstantiated sentence.

Madam Speaker, I am not the research team. I have quoted extensively from some very important research. I would like to point out to the hon. member, that he is close to my era, perhaps a decade or so away. I would like to suggest that at the C. D. Howe Institute, which I think is rather a credible institute, the observation has been made that the quality of instruction available to university students today is not nearly as good as that provided to their parents who attended Ontario universities 30 years ago.
I would suggest the hon. member falls into that category. I would also suggest that one of the reasons foreign students come here is because our universities are much less expensive. It has nothing to do with the quality of the university.
