speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am reluctant to start a speech in the circumstances because I am aware that at four o'clock we will probably be interrupted when the Prime Minister arrives. Perhaps in the meantime I could start. Having a captive audience of over half of the Cabinet is a particular treat for me as it is very rare, during debate, to see so many here and I am delighted.
I want to say that discussing Bill C-69, the act to restrain government expenditures, is a misguided effort on the part of the government. We hear constant complaints about how we never make suggestions on this side of the House. I can tell the ministers opposite, through you, Madam Speaker, that I have made many suggestions for measures to do with the economy, such as cutting the advertising budget on the goods and service tax, which would save millions and millions of dollars for the taxpayers of Canada every year, cutting the size of this Cabinet in half, which would reduce expenditures significantly and possibly increase the effectiveness. It could not reduce it.
I say that we could consider all these suggestions and yet, when I have made them, I have been blithely ignored. The Minister of Finance has not even come in and made a speech in response, agreed, or said that he would not agree to my suggestions. They have been politely and firmly ignored.
I am afraid that this attitude on the part of the government is regrettable, and particularly so when it is the educational facilities of Canada that are suffering as a result of the cuts that are proposed in Bill C-69.
My own community has in it two universities; one of which is not directly affected by these cuts since it is funded solely by the federal government, being the Royal Military College. The other university is directly affected, as indeed are all universities across this country.
I want to confine my remarks on Bill C-69 to the educational aspect of these cuts so the Minister of National Health and Welfare can relax.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I'm virtually comatose.

He says he is relaxed already. I suggest that if he and his colleagues had a proper interest in health care delivery in this country, they would not relax when they are trying to pass this particular bill through the House of Commons. He knows, as well as I do, that this bill will significantly reduce the ability of the provinces to fund health care in their jurisdictions as a result of the federal government trying to dump the problem to the provinces.
June 11, 1990

On March 14, 1989, the Canadian Association of University Teachers wrote to the Prime Minister to make him aware of their particular concerns regarding post-secondary funding. That association argued that the transfer of funds under the Established Programs Financing Act, "has a direct and profound impact on the quality of our universities and of our research effort". That is not me talking, it is not some other member of the opposition bleating, this is the Canadian Association of University Teachers expressing their concerns about these cuts. They ask the Prime Minister to show his support for post-secondary education by announcing, in the government's Speech from the Throne, a renewed commitment to education funding.
How did the Prime Minister respond to this request? What did he do to strengthen Canada's post-secondary institutions? In his April 1989 budget, the Minister of Finance reduced by 1 per cent the escalator provisions used to calculate the level of funding that each government receives through EPF. This was in keeping with his decision in 1986 to lower the escalator by 2 per cent.
Continuing this assault, the Prime Minister now plans, through this bill that we are now debating, to impose a two-year freeze on per capita EPF transfers to the provinces. He plans to remove the inflation protection from these transfers precisely when the new goods and services tax bill, which is now sitting in the other place will, on the finance department's own admission, cause a 1 per cent jump in inflation.
We in the opposition know that those projections are incorrect. It will be more than 1 per cent and yet that is what the Department of Finance is maintaining, you cut the transfers to the provinces while you increase the costs through your own taxation measures. That is unfair and that is what this government is doing by these bills.
In addition, the rate of growth of the transfers will be restricted to 3 percentage points below the rate of growth in the economy when the freeze is lifted after 1992. This will result in a further erosion and deterioration of the moneys available to provinces for education purposes. The cumulative results of this government's assault on EPF transfers has meant that from 1986 to 1995, provincial governments will have lost $8.9 billion in post-secondary education funding. Of this loss, approxi-
Govemment Orders
mately $2 billion, that is about a quarter of it, is attributable to Bill C-69 alone.
Back in 1984 when the Prime Minister's party was trying to get elected, it wrote to the Canadian Association of University Teachers in a newsletter that they were "committed to sustaining the current federal financial commitment according to the formula set out in the 1977 agreement. We believe that financing post-secondary education is an important priority for both levels of government". I note that that was before an election. How their tune changed after the election, after they duped the Canadian people into voting for them, they changed their tune and then began slashing and cutting all over the place. Talk about honesty in government, talk about the obligation to maintain your promises, this is a shocking record. Since 1984 the government's support of post-secondary education has become so weak that the Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada has projected that, as a result of Bill C-69 and the February 1990 budget, federal cash transfers in support of post-secondaiy education could disappear before the year 2000 in Ontario and before the year 2010 in the rest of the provinces.
The government's record fails to match its rhetoric and its promises. Instead of being given the straight goods on this bill and its effects, we are given fudged figures that cloud the issue and make it look as though this somehow is a bonanza for the provinces. It is not. The Canadian people know it is not and the government, in truth, knows it is not, but simply will not reveal the facts.
While the government has initiated some worth-while programs in the education field-
Name one.

My hon. friend from Winnipeg South Centre asks me to name one.
I must say I have not heard anyone over there suggest any because I do not think they know of them. But, in fairness, there has been an increase-and I will deliver a compliment-in the funding levels to the various research councils. On the other hand, the increase has been less in almost every case than the level of inflation. It is not much of an increase, but there has been some additional funding, and I am corrected every time I say that.

June 11, 1990
Routine Proceedings
The EPF cuts will reduce the effect of these few positive initiatives because there are several factors to be borne in mind in relation to university research. Perhaps hon. members opposite would like to learn something about it. First, research work in the universities incurs expenses not covered by research grants. If a university receives a grant to conduct certain research, it has to hire staff and provide space and facilities of various kinds for the researcher to do the work.
The report of the task force on federal policies and programs for technology development prepared by the ministry of state for science and technology in July 1984 stated: "Because most federal funding covers only the incremental research costs such as supplies, technicians' salaries and equipment, it is estimated that each grant dollar a university receives from Ottawa via the research councils forces it to spend at least another dollar on facilities and other overheads". There has been no increase in the funding for universities for overheads and increased costs of research facilities, none whatever. This is another item the government leaves off the plate. It announces with great trumpet and fanfare that it will increase funding for universities, but it does not pay the costs. It gives you a little dollop and says: "Here you go, this is funded. All this money has been paid". The government will not pay the increased costs to universities that are obliged to make up out of the dollars that come from the province through EPF transfers, dollars that are not now coming at the same rate. They have dropped and Bill 069 is one of the principal instruments by which these moneys dropped.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext: It depends on the provinces.

The hon. Minister for Science and Technology, who should know more about this than I do, says that it depends on the provinces. He should also know that the province of Ontario passes on the bulk of this money. I agree that perhaps the government of Premier Vander Zalm does not pass the money along to its universities, but that is a Social Credit government with close ties to the PC Party, and I am not surprised that it does not pass it on. Liberal governments are far less tight-fisted with the few federal dollars that they get from this minister.
Since it is the EPF transfers which pay for these other costs, it is obvious that cutting these transfers will mean that post-secondary institutions will not have the funds
they need to make effective use of the research and development grants that they are now receiving, both from this government and from the provincial governments.
Speaking at the University of Waterloo in 1987, the Prime Minister himself said these words: "I have been speaking and writing about the urgent and pressing necessity of increasing our national commitment to R and D, not only in the amounts we spend, but in the way we spend. We cannot be satisfied with what we have accomplished". He was certainly right there. Things have got worse at his behest since 1987. This government has cut what it accomplished before. How can he be satisfied today? He was not satisfied in 1987. The implication of his speech-and I note that this was before an election campaign in 1988-indicated that he was not satisfied and felt the situation should be improved. I notice that this improvement has not occurred. This bill makes the situation worse.
I urge the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology to plead with his colleague the Minister of Finance to withdraw this bill so that we can increase payments to the provinces, not cut, slash and reduce in the way in which the government proposed to do.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Before continuing, according to an order made with unanimous consent earlier today, I would say to the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands that he will understand the interruption. The hon. member will have the floor after the proceedings.

Mr. Speaker, it is with a sense of national pride that I rise to inform the House of the results of the recent First Ministers' conference.
Since I became leader of my party, I set out as one of my basic goals to bring Quebec back into the Canadian constitutional family. That goal is now within reach, and
June 11, 1990

if all goes well within the next few weeks that goal will become a permanent reality.
Hear, hear!

Once the three remaining legislatures pass the Meech Lake Accord, Quebec will formally rejoin our constitutional family and Canada will be able to face its future united and strong. We will then be able to address ourselves to some other constitutional issues. In particular, Senate reform. It is so important to so many Canadians in the east and in the west. We will be free to concentrate more of our time and attention on creating the requisite economic and social conditions for Canadians to prosper and for Canada to thrive.
There is, as we all know in this House, a new world to be won. Canada needs to turn the page, at last, on a long, and controversial and often debilitating period of our constitutional history so that we can move with firmness and confidence into the next century.

Mr. Speaker, I think that will soon be possible with the passage of the Meech Lake Accord as is. I have consistently said that Meech Lake must be passed by June 23 and that other constitutional concerns would be met subsequently. Anyone who carefully reads the document we signed will see that I kept my word and that my government kept its word to Quebec and Canada.
Hear, hear.

I kept my word on the accord and, Mr. Speaker, I will also keep my word on the other matters on which we reached agreement last week.
It was taking a chance with Canada's future when, in 1982, it was decided to go ahead with constitutional amendments without the assent of the National Assembly of Quebec. Isolating Quebec once was once too many as we all recognized. I resolved that it should never happen again in this country. For Quebecers, it was a bitter outcome to the 1980 referendum because the whole 1980-82 constitutional round was undertaken pursuant to a solemn undertaking, given just six days before the referendum vote, by the then Prime Minister of Canada on behalf of all of us who were members of the "Non" committee. At the time, the Prime Minister said, and he spoke for all Canadians, and very eloquently, I may say, and I quote: "We're telling you in the other
Routine Proceedings
provinces that we won't accept that a "Non" be interpreted by you as an indication that everything is fine and can remain as it was before." Well, Mr. Speaker, and I say this without malice, there is no doubt things did change, but it was not the renewed federalism Quebecers thought they voted for when they voted yes or no to Canada on May 20, 1980.
On August 6,1984, at Sept-Iles, I made a commitment to pursue Quebec's signature on the Canadian constitution, provided we could establish ground rules to meet the minimal conditions of success. Some people believed the 1980 referendum closed the books. As a Quebecer, however, I had my doubts, I had serious personal doubts. I saw it on the North Shore and I saw it throughout Quebec, and I thought that the sense of estrangement in Quebec was too deep and too broad to take the risk, because the 1981-82 process and its results had raised some serious questions throughout Quebec about the value of its ongoing association with Canada. I felt this was very unfortunate, because as a Quebecer, I have always thought that Quebec had a future, a brillant and dynamic future, within the Canadian federation. I was therefore very disturbed by what I heard across the province.
However, mindful of the sensitivity of this issue, we did not reopen the file until there was a federalist Premier in place in Quebec. My government decided to proceed with the reform process then because we did not think there would ever be more favourable circumstances for doing so. The harrowing memory of the Referendum was still fresh in people's minds, but a federalist government was and is today in office in Quebec: the Liberal government headed by Robert Bourassa. A spirit of reconciliation prevailed in federal-provincial relations. I refer now, Mr. Speaker, to 1986 and the beginning of 1987.

It was also obvious that the sense of alienation was not exclusive to Quebec in any way. The people in the east, west and north were also not satisfied with the status quo. Certainly, they appeared not to be. Without Quebec at the table, however, the result of the 1981-82 constitutional reform was effectively blocked. I saw that firsthand, and I discussed it with some of my NDP and Liberal colleagues in this House. We all saw it firsthand in 1985 when as Prime Minister of Canada I chaired the

June 11, 1990
Routine Proceedings
First Ministers' Conference seeking a constitutional amendment for aboriginal groups. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that we came within a whisker of success, but we eventually failed. I believe we would have succeeded, we would have avoided failure that day, had Quebec been participating fully in the Constitution, because the Government of Quebec had signalled clearly and publicly its support for the amendment.
Thus the first victims of 1981-82 were not Quebecers. They were our aboriginal peoples who should have received justice that day in 1985 and will now, with Quebec at the constitutional table, have an infinitely better chance at that justice they have been seeking so long.
Hear, hear.

At the same time my colleagues and I recognize that attempts to resolve all constitutional problems at once had generally failed in the past.
On July 14, 1986 I therefore wrote to the premiers suggesting that "the only realistic way I believe to proceed is, first, to bring Quebec back into the fold and to undertake a more extensive revision of the Constitution at a later stage".
The premiers agreed and, at their conference in August of 1986, the premiers of Canada issued the Edmonton Declaration. By that declaration, under the chairmanship of Premier Getty, they "agreed that their top constitutional priority" was "to embark immediately upon a federal-provincial process, using Quebec's five proposals as a basis for discussion, to bring about Quebec's full and active participation in the Canadian federation". They also agreed that other matters would be dealt with in a subsequent round.
Over the fall of 1986 and the winter of 1987, Senator Lowell Murray and his officials began a long, difficult and time consuming series of consultations with their provincial colleagues and with all others in Canada interested in the process, for example with aboriginal groups, with women's groups, and with those advancing the cause of special interests.
In April of 1987,1 invited the premiers to Meech Lake to see, as I said in my Law Day Address on April 15,
1987, if we could reach an agreement or whether it was better "to close the books" on the entire question.
I wanted it clear before we got to Meech Lake that we were not engaging with parti pris but that we were going to take a hard look at it, examine it carefully in an objective atmosphere with all the best possibilities for success, but that if it did not work they would have to decide whether it was not better in those circumstances to cut it off once and for all.
I said then that to reach agreement would "require us to find an appropriate balance between the principle of the equality of all the provinces and the need to protect them and enhance the distinctiveness Quebec brings to Canada".
On April 30, 1987, as hon. members know, the first ministers met at Meech Lake and reached an agreement in principle. Over the next weeks, legal experts from all governments developed a constitutional test.
On June 2, 1987, first ministers met at the Langevin Block and agreed upon a legal document that incorporated improvements that met the concerns that had arisen in the interim. On June 3,1987, the premiers and I signed the Meech Lake Accord.
The accord itself resulted from an obvious process of give and take. On that morning of June 3, 1987, I genuinely doubt, Mr. Speaker, if it had occurred to any of us that we would still be talking about this three years later. But then three governments changed and commitments that had been given were re-opened.
It is against this background that we have tried to create a new consensus, one that respected the Meech Lake framework while responding to concerns that have been raised in many cases quite unexpectedly over the subsequent or intervening three years. As members know, we have spared no effort to bring the dissenting provinces into the Meech consensus, while responding to their sincere concerns and to those of many Canadians that have arisen from both the process and the substance at Meech Lake.
The House established a special committee under the chairmanship of the member for Sherbrooke, the hon. Jean Charest, to conduct hearings on the New Brunswick proposal.
The Charest committee reported on May 17.1 want to take this opportunity to thank all members from all parties of the Charest committee who worked so hard
June 11, 1990

and who gave such devotion to Canada, all members from all parties. This was a remarkable contribution, and in underlining the tremendous work-

-done, not just for Canada but for Quebec, by the Hon. Jean Charest, I also wish to express my unqualified appreciation for all members of all parties in this House.
Hear, hear.

I wish to thank in particular the Leader of the Opposition, Mr. Gray, and the Leader of the New Democratic Party, Ms. McLaughlin, for the sensitivity of their approach and for support they and members of their parties, some of whom I see on the front benches and elsewhere in this House, accorded the government on this issue of crucial national importance.
I wish to offer special thanks to Mr. Turner and Mr. Broadbent for the leadership they have provided on this issue from the very beginning. Canadians will remember that Mr. Turner never wavered from his deeply held conviction that the accord was right for Canada and that Canadian unity took priority over political considerations. Mr. Broadbent likewise stood firm in defence of the accord and deployed his considerable energy and persuasiveness on behalf of its adoption.
In retrospect, it is very clear to me that the success we achieved last weekend would not have been possible without the leadership and the support in the very beginning of John Turner and Ed Broadbent.
I want to thank as well all of those Canadians who helped so much in our darkest hours to keep the struggle for Meech Lake alive. Editorialists, constitutional experts, scholars, students, working mothers, and mill workers all contributed highly to our initiative.
In this past week in Ottawa the problems were complex and the disagreements were very, very difficult to narrow, but the premiers and I persevered for seven long days-it seemed like years-and bridged the differences and worked out an agreement. None of them had an illusions about the stakes involved.
Routine Proceedings
Premiers Peterson, Bourassa, Buchanan, Vander Zalm, Ghiz, Devine, and Getty remained true to their vision of Canada and despite enormous political pressures stood by their original endorsement of the Meech Lake Accord.
Premier McKenna will be tabling the Meech Lake Accord and two companion documents in his legislature this week. Premier Filmon will be initiating the ratification process by convening public hearings shortly. Premier Wells phoned me earlier today to indicate that he will be submitting the accord for a free vote in the Newfoundland House of Assembly.
According to the terms of the agreement reached in Ottawa, Saturday, he will use every possible effort to achieve a decision prior to June 23, 1990. Once the accord is adopted, the Governor General will be advised to proclaim the amendment and the Meech Lake Accord will at last be entrenched in the Constitution and Quebecers can feel truly part of this great Canada.
Since the accord was signed three years ago, concerns have been raised by women, native people, northern Canadians, and minority language groups. The premiers and I heard these concerns. We have committed ourselves to seek approval as soon as possible by Parliament and the provincial legislatures of constitutional amendments directed to them.
We have agreed to make it explicit that the equality of the sexes is fully protected under the Constitution of Canada. We have also agreed that First Ministers' Conferences on aboriginal constitutional matters be held every three years, and that representatives of Canada's aboriginal peoples and territorial governments participate in the conferences at the invitation of the Prime Minister of Canada.
With respect to the territories, we all agreed that they be empowered, like the provinces, to submit names for consideration when vacancies occur in the Senate of Canada and the Supreme Court of Canada. It was also agreed that representatives of the territorial governments participate at annual constitutional and economic conferences in discussions of issues that, in the judgment of the Prime Minister of Canada, directly affect them.
We agreed to address the options for provincehood for Yukon and the Northwest Territories in future constitutional discussions. Agreement was also reached on

June 11, 1990
Routine Proceedings
adding issues of interest to English and French speaking linguistic minorities to the agenda of constitutional conferences. It is most important that it never be forgotten that the protection of linguistic minorities remains a fundamental obligation of the Parliament and the people of Canada.
It was agreed that the equality of the two linguistic communities of New Brunswick be reflected in the Constitution.
We have further agreed to accelerate the process of Senate reform. After proclamation of the Meech Lake Accord, a commission will be established comprising federal, provincial and territorial government representatives to conduct hearings and to report to Parliament and provincial legislatures prior to the First Ministers' Conference on Senate Reform to be held in British Columbia by the end of this year.
The commission will make proposals to give effect to the following objectives. The first is that the Senate should be elected. Second, it should provide for more equitable representation of the less populous provinces and the territories. The third is that the Senate should have effective powers to ensure the interests of residents of the less populous provinces and territories figure more prominently in national decision making, reflect Canadian duality, and strengthen the Government of Canada's capacity to govern on behalf of all citizens, while preserving the principle of the responsibility of the government to the House of Commons. I have undertaken to report semi-annually to this House on progress toward Senate reform.
First ministers agreed to seek adoption of an amendment on comprehensive Senate reform by July 1, 1995. If, by then, comprehensive Senate reform has not been achieved, Senate representation will be amended automatically pursuant to a formula that we have all agreed upon.
Premier Peterson, on behalf of Ontario, proposed that his province relinquish six Senate seats. Premier Buchanan and Premier McKenna joined in this nation building gesture in giving up two Senate seats each. These 10 seats would be distributed to the four western provinces and to Newfoundland and Labrador, bringing their representation in the Senate to eight senators each, the
same number as Nova Scotia and New Brunswick would then have once the modifications are in full play.
This provides for some rebalancing of Senate representation in favour of the less populous provinces in case Senate reform is not achieved by the target date, and notwithstanding the tremendous pressures that we have placed upon ourselves, on the institutions, and on members of this House to pursue very actively the objectives of legitimate and thoughtful Senate reform.
With respect to a statement of constitutional recognitions, we took note of the repeated unsuccessful attempts over the last 20 years to draft a text acceptable to all concerned. We agreed, as part of our future constitutional agenda, to refer drafts submitted by the Government of Canada and by the Governments of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Ontario, and British Columbia to an all-party committee of the House of Commons for public hearings starting July 16.
A report on the substance and the appropriate placement of the clause in the Constitution will be prepared for the consideration of first ministers at their constitutional conference later this year.
This, Mr. Speaker, in brief is a general outline of the main elements of the agreement.
With respect to the relationship of the distinct society clause in the Meech Lake Accord with the Charter of Rights, the concerns of Canadians were heard by the First Ministers and were considered with great care. The advice of eminent counsel was solicited. Based on that advice, First Ministers concluded that no amendment was required. We sought that advice to reassure all Canadians of our commitment to the Charter. For that reason, the opinion of counsel was appended to the communique.
In re-integrating into the constitutional family, Quebecers are saying yes to the statement of values contained in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. In its April 3, 1989, Speech from the Throne, the Government of Canada committed itself to strengthening the Charter of Rights and Freedoms in future constitutional negotiations. Accordingly, we welcome the commitment of all First Ministers to a continuing review of the Constitution and the Charter as part of the process of annual First Ministers' Conferences on the Constitution.
June 11, 1990

With respect to the amending process that we followed this past week, Canadians should know that by and large it is the same process that was followed in 1987, in 1982 and, indeed, with some variations all the way back to Charlottetown in 1865. We did not invent the process of the last few weeks or the last few years. We very clearly inherited a process. This process has proven to be increasingly unsatisfactory in several respects and must be changed.
There should, first and foremost, be ample opportunity for Canadians to participate in the process. I propose today that we change the rules of this House so that once this chapter in our constitutional evolution is over public hearings will in future become mandatory in advance of all constitutional amendments so that the people of Canada will truly be heard.
Hear, hear!

Another aspect of the process that must be changed is that set out by Article 39(2) of the 1982 Constitution. That is the clause that mandated the three-year ratification period. In retrospect, it is obvious that that length of time makes our reaching agreement more difficult rather than facilitates it. Even if you are Harry Houdini, you could not get it done, and that must be changed.
Hear, hear!

With respect to the spending power, I wish to state unequivocally that neither the Meech Lake Accord nor the agreement reached here last week diminishes the federal government's commitments on regional disparities and equalization-including programs to pursue the commitments set out in Section 36(1) of the Constitution Act of 1982.

Mr. Speaker, we should soon be able to turn the page on this chapter of constitutional reform but we must not forget some of the lessons we learned from it. It is clear that there are serious misunderstandings in this country that we cannot afford to ignore. And so I appeal to all Canadians to join us in healing the damage in the months ahead. We need to rebuild a sense of community and, especially, to promote more contact amongst Canadians right across this country. On one level, we need to recapture the sense of tolerance and common interest
Routine Proceedings
and common purpose that lies at the root of our success as a nation. At another level, we need to reaffirm the advantages we enjoy as a bilingual, multicultural country in a shrinking world.
My government will take a series of national policy initiatives that will both help to refurbish national unity and respond to the economic and social needs of all Canadians. At a time when it is becoming increasingly important to have a knowledge and an understanding of foreign cultures and international affairs, Canada is in a unique position to promote its own interests while helping developing countries. While western Europe is merging into a new, supra-national entity, eastern Europe is undergoing rapid change, Asia is experiencing spectacular growth, democracy is taking root in Latin America and economic development in Africa is at a standstill, Canada has interests to promote and a remarkable contribution to make.
Blest with one of the strongest economies in the world, Canada is part of a handful of countries that have a real and decisive impact on the international scene. I have said before, in other circumstances-

We do not want to make Canada a superpower; we just want to make Canada a super country.
Hear, hear!

However, Mr. Speaker, all this would be impossible if we were not a united country.
As a Quebecer myself, I appeal to all Quebecers to join in the healing process. With the passage of the Meech Lake Accord, Quebec will achieve our essential objective: security for its cultural and linguistic distinctiveness. Quebec finally returns to the Canadian family by the front door. It was my dearest dream, because I could not conceive of Canada in all its splendour without Quebec. Today, Quebecers and all Canadians continue together again on the path to a brillant future.

Let us co-operate to reinforce the ties that bind this great country together.

June 11, 1990
Routine Proceedings
Over the past several months, Canadians have said with one voice that they want to remain together in one Canada united and strong from St. John's to Victoria to the Arctic Islands. We have our differences in this country, even from time to time as we have them in this House.
But the history of Canada is one of perseverance and co-operation and tolerance. It is a history of aboriginal peoples, two major language groups and the multicultural mosaic, all seeking to respect each other's differences and each other's convictions.
I always felt that the greatest attribute of Canadian citizenship was the tolerance that it brought to each and every one of us, tolerance for minority groups, respect for others' religions, respect for others' values however different from our own, respect for the values that are brought to this country, to our shores by immigrants from all over the world. Canada began that way, and we have been enriched decade after decade. If we maintain that kind of vision, that kind of openness and that kind of spirit Canada will always remain a land of tolerance and opportunity. That is the commitment I am sure that exists on behalf of all members of all parties of this House of Commons.
Hear, hear!

Because from our pluralism comes a tolerant society, a society that is ready to look out on the world again, rather than in onto itself, unfailingly.
The challenge of nation-building did not end with the BNA Act in 1867. It did not end with patriation and the Charter in 1982. It did not end with the Meech Lake Accord. Nation-building is much more than writing a constitution. It continues every day in this House and in your house-in the cities, towns, villages and farms across this country. It is an act of the heart. May it ever be so.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like most Canadians, my colleagues and I closely followed the efforts of the Prime Minister and the provincial premiers in recent days to seek a resolution to the present constitutional impasse. We believe that the final communique signed by the provincial premiers and the Prime Minister this past weekend can
provide the basis for the successful resolution of that constitutional impasse.

We understand the importance of the 1987 constitutional amendment, the purpose of which was to make Quebec a full member of the constitutional family. With Quebec back in, we can fully discuss all the constitutional changes being called for by groups and regions throughout our country.

We regret, however, that the Prime Minister waited so long to call a meeting of First Ministers. Canadians, generally, will recall that we on this side of the House have been calling for a First Ministers Conference for some months.
We believed that only when the provincial premiers and the Prime Minister were sitting and talking together at the same table would the dynamic arise that could lead to a breakthrough. We believe that the Prime Minister's delay contributed to the crisis atmosphere that pervaded the recent discussions among the premiers and himself.
Hear, hear!

This unfortunate crisis atmosphere has led to a situation whereby there is very little time for the provinces who have not yet approved the 1987 constitutional amendment to do so by June 23.
Another result of the Prime Minister's approach has been that the discussions have not been as open as they might have been. Therefore, the public feels that they have been excluded from the process. We share the concern of Canadians about the process that took place last week and about its lack of openness. Canadians feel, and rightly so, that they have been excluded from a process that affects their future and the future of their country.
We were encouraged, therefore, that the Prime Minister and the provincial premiers have identified the need to review the procedure for amending the Constitution.
We agree with Canadians that never again should we undergo this kind of stressful process. We believe that open public discussion and debate are essential to constitutional change.
June 11, 1990

Furthermore, we believe that, had the Prime Minister himself shown more leadership and begun to seek a resolution of the constitutional impasse sooner, rather than waiting for the proposals of Premier McKenna, we might well have resolved this matter some time ago. After all, constitutional negotiations are not labour negotiations.
Also, the Prime Minister spoke of taking steps to cure and to heal the divisions and damage that have arisen in our country in recent months. Canadians will recognize and remember what we consider to be the responsibility of the Prime Minister, the responsibility he must bear for the development of the unfortunate situation he now calls upon all of us to help cure.
[Translation\
Elear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I hope that the New Brunswick, Manitoba and Newfoundland legislatures will accept this agreement and thereby will approve the 1987 constitutional amendment before June 23.

In his televised address to the nation on March 22, 1990, in response to the proposals of the Premier of New Brunswick, the Prime Minister said: "I know" that the accord "is not perfect." That is what he said. In fact, in 1987, we submitted a number of amendments which we believe would have strengthened and enriched the accord. We believe, if the Prime Minister had listened us to us seriously three years ago, that we might not have ended up in the current impasse.
The process of nation building in Canada is never easy. It is never complete. It is an ongoing challenge which faces every government and every individual elected to a position of trust in the country.

Mr. Speaker, we have succeeded in building a stronger, more united Canada by listening to the Canadian people and trying to meet their needs. We will reach consensus through dialogue and discussion. But to do so, Canadians across the land must become active participants.
Routine Proceedings

This country, in order to exist, needs all its people and all its regions. We need each other to build the kind of country we want for ourselves and our children. We need the people of Quebec, just as we need the people of Atlantic Canada, Ontario, the west and the north.
Everyone in this country must realize, yet again, that Canada is greater than the sum of its parts. Canada is worth preserving and must be preserved. If the country stays together, anything and everything is possible by way of constructive change and improvement in our Constitution and the way we live together.
We are all aware, for example, of the constitutional concerns of women, aboriginal people, minority language groups, multicultural groups, and the north, as well as of those calling for a reformed Senate. If Canada does not remain united, everything we have been discussing by way of reform of our institutions and the enhancement of our identity as Canadians will be meaningless and irrelevant.
The pressures that we saw last week at the conference centre in Ottawa have been transferred from the premiers and the Prime Minister to the members of the legislatures of Newfoundland, New Brunswick, and Manitoba. The members of those legislatures now have the burden and the responsibility for the future of the 1987 accord and what it could mean for the future of our country. I am sure they take these responsibilities veiy seriously.
I was very impressed by the words of Clyde Wells, the Premier of Newfoundland, to his legislature, the House of Assembly of Newfoundland, this morning. He said: "I am confident that the members of this honourable House, and indeed all Newfoundlanders and Labrado-rans, will express their views on the basis of their own sincere convictions and with the future of Canada foremost in their minds and hearts."
These are wise words, words of sincerity and conviction. Let these words serve as inspiration for all of us here in the House and for all Canadians. Let us always put the future of Canada foremost in our minds and our hearts.

Hear, hear.

June 11, 1990
Routine Proceedings

Mr. Speaker, as I rise to respond to the Prime Minister's statement today and as we watched the events of the last week and saw the kind of pressures and stress that the First Ministers and the Prime Minister underwent-and all of those who were not a part of that process underwent-certainly, I am not here to criticize those people who were involved, but to say constructively that we have to be honest and say that the process has not been a great reconciliation. It has been a possible accommodation.
I appreciate the Prime Minister's comments on process and I, too, would like to address that as well. As I begin, I want to state clearly that the New Democratic Party sees constitutional negotiation from the first principle that we must work to strive for the unity of the country.
As a party, we have consistently supported the five principles put forward by Quebec, including the distinct society. We also accept that the current round of constitutional negotiations were primarily to bring Quebec into the Constitution.

We heard many passionate speeches last week. Unfortunately, the constitutional process rarely gives concrete expression to the deep love these many participants showed for our country.

As I have watched the constitutional process unfold over the past few years, I have come to the conclusion that too often we fail to come to terms with our identity as a nation. We fail to take that unique identity and turn it into a constitution that will guide us over the next few years, the next decade, and beyond. After this week, what we and all Canadians have seen is that we have to rethink that process of doing that. The process of executive federalism that we saw in action this week has been shown in some ways to be a flawed process. We must re-examine that.

Before embarking on a difficult and divisive constitutional process, we did not mange to achieve a national consensus on the identity of Canada.

People look at Canada and define it by our identity as a vast northern country, with the Yukon and the Northwest Territories; the existence of two separate groups in the country, identified by the distinctiveness of Quebec, its language and its culture; the existence of aboriginal people as a vital part of our society as the first nations of the country; and, the emerging nature of our multicultural and our multi-racial society.
Hear, hear!

I deeply believe that our national identity, as defined by the characteristics I just mentioned, must be the basis of our Constitution. Even if we accept that this was the Quebec round of negotiations, and we do, some clauses of the Meech Lake Accord do not take into account the aspirations of other people and groups, in particular the North, native people, women and ethnic groups.
There has been talk of closing the circle of Confederation. I strongly hope that the signature of Quebec allowing Quebec to be a full participant in the Constitution that we saw on Saturday will begin that process, but the circle of Confederation will not be closed until the aboriginal people, northerners, women, and all Canadians become participants in the constitutional process.
The Prime Minister spoke to a commitment to opening up that process. I remind the Prime Minister that in this document it is the Prime Minister who has the ability to say when the territories and aboriginal people shall be present at the table. I will urge the Prime Minister-and I will continue to raise this issue with him-that aboriginal people and the territories be full participants in First Ministers' Conferences.
Particularly, Mr. Speaker, I want to mention that I hope when the first ministers meet in 1990 on the Canada clause aboriginal people are there when their rights are being discussed.
About a month ago the Charest report was released. It seems as quickly as that report was put together as a result of public hearings-it was in a short time frame- it heard about 160 witnesses. It was also the result of the hearing of some 800 briefs and presentations. The report was signed and endorsed by all parties. The Charest committee had a process and a result that we New Democrats could endorse.
June 11, 1990

Government Orders
However, it seems that in this process we had two parallel activities going on: the Charest report on one hand and the events of last week that we must say bore little or no relationship to each other.

The recommendations of the Charest Report are very similar to those the New Democratic Party made in 1987. Its recommendations are almost identical to a resolution the NDP adopted last December in Winnipeg.

The NDP has fought consistently for improvements to Meech Lake, recognizing and accepting the five important principles of Quebec. The agreement signed on Saturday that we are talking about today contains some of those improvements but not all. The victory has been at least getting the concerns on the table and in having the discussions take place.
I want to remind all members of this House that the issues of the aboriginal people, women, multi-racial and multi-heritage communities did not get on the table just because of us. They got on the table because those groups stood up and demanded to be heard. Now we as politicians must listen to those voices and ensure that they are incorporated in future constitutional talks.
In the strongest possible terms I want to say that as much as we appreciated that those issues were on the table for discussion and appear in this communique, my party and I cannot endorse the process as it took place last week.
What we witnessed was a nation literally with its faces pressed against the glass of the TV to try to get some bit of information not just about the future of the Constitution but about the future of the country. We saw women and aboriginal people marching outside the Conference Centre waiting as 11 people decided their fate, but they were not included.
We saw the elected Premier of Yukon and the elected Government Leader of the Northwest Territories on the outside of those negotiations and not included. We did not see openness. We did not see openness, we did not see consultation, and we did not see a public process.

I was saddened and discourged by the attempt I saw last week to reject the process and the accord. I do not reject the accord; it is the process I reject.
I do not reject the accord because the unity of this country has become the key concern. We must go beyond constitutional discussions and deal with other issues.
In conclusion, while I feel sad and discouraged, I say yes to the imperfect agreement reached last week. I cannot accept the events that took place last week.

I appreciate the Prime Minister's comment about mandatory public consultation, but we must also listen to those consultations and include their results in the final resolution. All of us must work, as politicians and as Canadians, to bring this country together.
The discussions on the future of our country have not ended. Let us strive as a united country to include all Canadians from sea to sea to sea in these discussions.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, with the permission of all hon. members of the House and pursuant to their remarks and mine, I would like to table the document called The First Ministers' Meeting on the Constitution: Final Communique, June 9, 1990.

With a French version, of course, to match the English, "The First Ministers' Meeting on the Constitution: Final Communique, June 9, 1990."

Mr. Speaker, before I was interrupted by that tumultuous round of applause, I was speaking about the cuts in transfer payments to the provinces as contemplated in Bill C-69. I am sony that the Minister of Transport is otherwise occupied.
As I was indicating, the cutting of these EPF transfers will hurt universities and colleges in many other ways. I would like to list some of them. First, the lack of funds will mean that new buildings will not be built, causing further overcrowding of both students and faculty. This overcrowding will force universities to start restricting employment levels, thereby reducing accessibility to higher education in Canada.
The lack of funds will mean that laboratories will not be updated and modernized and that library budgets will be too meagre to meet demands placed on libraries by students and faculty. Schools will not have the funds to hire new faculty. Thus the student-teacher ratio, which has increased dramatically over the last few years, will continue to increase.
For example, while the number of full-time university and college students in Canada increased by 31 per cent from 1977 to 1988, the number of full-time professors has increased by only 10.5 per cent. While everyone realizes that there has been more part-time faculty, the fact is that more full-time faculty has not been retained in the numbers that are commensurate with the increase in enrolment.
Despite the increase in enrolment, this government is slashing EPF transfers to the provinces, thereby debilitating the province's ability to pay the money to these universities and colleges. In fact, according to the estimates of the Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada, about one-fifth of all federal program spending reductions over the next five years, as announced in the February 20 budget, will fall on transfers that are in support of post-secondary education.
Of course, with this government we can expect more cuts. The figure may be inaccurate because maybe in next year's budget we will have even more. At the moment, that is the way it looks from the figures that the Minister of Finance presented, as analysed by the Association of Universities and Colleges.
In addition to those policies, this government is pursuing the goods and services tax. This bill is one that the goods and services tax will affect in that, in addition to cutting the payment to the provinces as I previously indicated, the beneficiaries of those payments will now be paying out additional funds in the form of the goods and services tax. For some of those reasons the government of Alberta has taken a firm stand against this tax. It has recently come to my attention that the it has published the book Protecting Alberta's Future, Why We Oppose the Federal Goods and Services Tax.
The book is a government publication and I urge you to read it. It is published under the name of the Hon. Don Getty, Premier of the province of Alberta, and the Hon. Dick Johnston, the Treasurer of that province. It talks about the evils of the goods and services tax, evils we have been preaching about in this House. Unfortunately our pleas have fallen on deaf ears with respect to this matter and in terms of the government listening to us.
Here we have a case where the premier of one of the provinces has gone to the length of publishing a pamphlet outlining his difficulties with this tax. The disappointing thing is that the members from Alberta in this House have not been able to echo their premier's views on the goods and services tax. We have not heard about this publication from those members. Why have they not been criticizing this tax the way we have been when their own premier says that the tax is no good.
The only two members I have heard suggest that the goods and services tax is bad and ought not to proceed are now sitting on this side of the House as independents, the hon. member for Calgary Northeast and the hon. member for Calgary Southeast. And I understand the only reason they are sitting there is because they got the heave ho from the Conservative caucus. I see the whip is here, and I am surprised he would have countenanced this particular injustice to those members who, after all, were seeking to represent the interests of their premier in his opposition to this tax as outlined in this book.
I am not going to quote extensively from the book but I am sure that the arguments advanced in it are ones that support our objections to the goods and services tax. I am delighted to see we have an ally in the form of a Conservative premier in the province of Alberta. I am

very sorry that the Conservative members from Alberta do not feel free to speak their minds on this issue and criticize this tax.
I would enjoy hearing from the parliamentary secretary, or any of the other members from Alberta. I know that we have the views of two on the record.
Let me summarize again, going back to Bill C-69 and our problems with this bill.
We have a case where the government is cutting the transfers to the provinces for education. I have to ask the question, are these policies of cut, cut, cut, slash, slash, slash that the government has engaged in those of a government which has a clear vision of its country, a clear vision for the future for educational purposes of its young citizens? I suggest it is not.
Would a government with foresight and intelligence seeking to invest in the country's future pass legislation like Bill C-69? I suggest it would not. It would not even propose it.
I suggest that the government is not interested in securing our future through education. Instead, it is determined to cut the deficit at all costs without taking into consideration any of the long-term ramifications of its actions. I suggest it is cutting the deficit of our country in the wrong place.
How is this country supposed to compete in the world? We keep hearing from the Prime Minister that under the free trade deal Canada will move forward to greater competition in the world and will do extremely well and we will prosper under this deal.
How can we do that if we cut back on education payments, if we cut back on the amount of money that we invest in our young people. This particular government seems indifferent to that fact, notwithstanding its boasting about the free trade agreement.
What we are doing by these cuts is saying to our universities and colleges: "Cut back your enrolment, reduce the number of students, lower the quality of your education because we cannot afford to pay on the basis we have been paying in the past." That is the message the government is sending and I suggest it is the wrong message and it ought not to be sending it.

It is saying that for libraries and student facilities in universities, cut back. We cannot afford to have lavish expenditures on libraries; we cannot afford expenditures on classrooms and laboratories; we are going to have to cram more students into the space. You are going to have to cut back on enrolment; you are going to have to provide less faculty, fewer books, fewer quality books, and so on. That is the message the government sends. Cut, cut, cut.
I suggest it is doing it in the wrong area. The country cannot compete if it is restricted to its old ways. The government is cutting initiative with this bill. Madam Speaker, it is delightful to hear the hon. member for Ontario cite statistics showing the wonderful record of the Liberal government in office in Ontario. Like him, I am delighted that I live in a province which is blessed with a government that cares for the people, that believes in education, that believes in the importance of education for its people, and delivers on its promises.
The Ontario government of Premier Peterson promised in the last campaign that it would improve educational opportunities, that it would reduce the deficit in Ontario and bring the Ontario economy into a surplus position. It has delivered on its promises. What a comparison to the government that he supports in this House. It has a most disgraceful record of broken promises right down the line.
The hon. member says Ontario should help with the federal deficit. The responsibility for the federal deficit should be shouldered by the government here in this House, not by cutting transfers to the provinces. I think he may have missed the boat. He cited the example of the province that is best able to maintain itself in spite of these cuts. The purpose of the transfers is to equalize opportunity across Canada. If we cut transfer payments to provinces that cannot afford to maintain educational facilities without these moneys, we are going to make it extremely difficult for them to match the opportunities available in Ontario.
The purpose of transfer payments is to equalize opportunity across Canada. Cutting the transfer payments is not equalizing, it is destabilizing. It is unequalizing because, in a province that does not have the financial resources the province of Ontario happens to have at the moment, the educational programs cannot be maintained on that basis.
I urge the hon. member, if he thinks the payments that have been increased on education in Ontario are so great, to go to the universities and colleges and ask what they are getting in the circumstances. They are being faced with additional costs imposed by the province of Ontario and the federal government that have to be paid out of the 7 per cent increase given to education. They
have to pay the goods and services tax but of those funds starting next January. It is fine to say that education is exempt but there are many things that are not exempt, and the hon. member knows that. That will have to be taken out of the 7 per cent.
There are, in addition, the increases in the unemployment insurance that this government has imposed through its budget. Those payments are made by the universities and colleges in respect of all their employees at very significant additional cost to them.
In addition, there is the new provincial tax which has replaced the OHIP premiums and the employment tax in Ontario which will have to be paid. There is additional money to be paid for equalization programs within the colleges and universities to bring wage rates for women in the universities into line with those paid to men. Those programs are also costing a significant sum to colleges.
So even if they were to receive a full 7 per cent, before they can start allocating that money, statutory claims on that money will reduce the effective rate to a very low one. I am not being critical of the province of Ontario, but the 7 per cent is barely enough to keep any progress going in universities and colleges in Ontario.
If the hon. member would take the time to meet with some heads of colleges and discuss these issues with them, I am sure he would find, as I have, that the situation is much worse than he describes, that money is urgently required.
The cuts proposed by the government in Bill C-69 are seriously hurting the ability of the province of Ontario to make the payments that are required to these places of learning when they are facing the Draconian measures imposed by this government. It is time to stop this whittling away of the transfers, to change this policy around and to get this bill out of here.

Tory times are tough times for some people, but if you happen to be a privileged person like John Crow these are very good times. What is sinister about this is that we do not know the facts. This is all secret. We cannot get the information. This ought not to be the case.
We also find out that while the heads of our largest Crown corporations are telling their employees to take cuts in pay or make very modest demands, they are giving themselves some nice increases. One of the vice-presidents of CN, while asking his employees to take a 4 per cent increase in pay, himself last year took a 39 per cent increase in pay. This is an example of don't do as I do, do as I say.
This is to say nothing about some of our senior public servants. The Minister of Finance is saying that we have got to hold the line, yet some of our senior public servants were getting increases over the past three years of 31 per cent.
There is a lot the government could cut. It could cut the size of cabinet. It could cut the size of the Prime Minister's Office, the largest PMO in Canadian history in terms of personnel. It could certainly make cuts to the government propaganda that we are bombarded with almost on a weekly basis telling us how good the GST is and so on.
Speaking of cuts, what about cutting some of the breaks that our large, profitable corporate friends receive? This is not a criticism of our large corporate friends. It is a criticism of the government that permits
Government Orders
thousands and thousands of large, profitable corporations to pay no income tax at all year after year.
Since those corporations do not pay any income tax at all, the government has to get some money some place. What does it do? It uses Bill C-69 to attack the sick and students by curtailing funds to our hospitals and post-secondary institutions.
You can gather from my comments, Mr. Speaker, that we do not support this bill. The New Democratic Party is opposed to this bill. As was every single witness who appeared before the committee, we are in complete and total opposition to this course of madness. That is the only way I can describe it.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was interested in listening to the member for Kamloops and his usual erudite comments, but I was listening in vain. I sat here waiting and waiting for the magic formula that I was expecting to come out in this speech, that is, his clarion call to the other place to reject this bill when it gets there.
I know there is another step that has to be taken first, but he and I know that we get out-voted in this House on a fairly regular basis. We oppose this bill and the New Democratic Party opposes this bill, but it seems that in spite of our pleas many of the government members will vote for this bill.
I know that the member has found a new interest in the Senate. His party has changed its policy on the Senate. It no longer wants to abolish the Senate. It wants to preserve the Senate. It supports the Senate. It wants the Senate to chuck out government bills right, left, and centre. I wonder if it is now his party's view that the Senate ought to reject this bill if and when it gets there. I wonder if he could tell us about that.
Just so that he does not have to concentrate on one question that he might find a little embarrassing, I will ask a second one. The second question he could deal with is about the recent increases in Public Service and Crown corporation salaries which in the view of our party, as discussed today in Question Period, far exceed the wage rates the government is paying to other employees and far exceed the government's own guidelines. I wonder if he would care to comment on government waste in this regard as well.

June 11, 1990

Mr. Speaker, I am always pleased to respond to my hon. friend from Kingston and the Islands. His questions are not necessarily that thoughtful, often, but interesting nevertheless.
Let's tackle the last one first. He asked me what I feel about the increases that senior managers at the deputy minister level, including their bonuses, received in the last year or so.
I was looking at a graph which shows that over the past three years deputy ministers and senior managers received compensation increases of 31.2 per cent. To be fair, that is not across the board, but to a select number of the senior mandarins in our system. That is not bad, Mr. Speaker, when you consider that over that period of time almost everybody else received about a 10 per cent increase. The deputy ministers and senior managers received in excess of 30 per cent.
It is that kind of symbolism that bothers people. While the government states that it is trying to hold the line, we find out that there were many senior officials who received these huge increases in pay.
This is not an increase to a salary of $30,000, nothing of the sort. Quite the contrary. As a matter of fact, if we compare the rates of our senior civil service to those in the United States, ours are significantly higher. They are getting increases and bonuses on top of relatively high salaries to begin with. However, that is only one small area, but symbolically valuable.
More appropriate is what happened in the Bank of Canada, where all of the senior staff got huge increases, including the Governor of the Bank of Canada himself. That was what bothered people most.
My hon. friend talks about his friends in the Senate, the persons who just voted themselves a $153 a day bonus to show up for work. If they simply show up and sit there, they get $153 on top of all their other regular pay.
I want to clarify a point that my hon. friend made. He was not certain whether or not I oppose the Senate. He will remember very vividly, I suspect, just a few days ago when we had a vote in the House of Commons, and I might say at the NDP's urging, questioning whether we should even vote to provide operating funds for the Senate. We raised this and we decided to have a vote on
providing operating funds for the Senate. I noticed with interest that all of the Conservatives voted in favour of supplying that money to the Senate to enable them to operate. All the Liberals in the House that day voted in favour of support for the Senate, but no New Democrats. The New Democrats voted unanimously against supplying a single cent of operating money for the Senate.
I do not know how much clearer you can get in terms of how you feel about the Senate.
But you want them to stop the GST?

No. I said our position is to vote at every opportunity no money for the Senate. The fact that they are sitting there and are now getting an extra $153 a day, let them do something, particularly the Liberals over there, because the majority of the people in the Senate right now are Liberal appointees. We think that the Liberals sometimes speak two languages. I would not say double speak-yes I would, double speak.
On the one hand, they say that they are opposed to the GST, but I guess they did not mean the Liberals in the Senate were opposed to the GST. The Liberals here voted against it, but already in the Senate the Liberals have voted in favour, in principle, of the 7 per cent goods and services tax. We are suggesting to those Liberals in the Senate to do what their colleagues in the House of Commons did and vote against the GST, because it means that the bill will be killed. We will save the taxpayers of Canada an incredible nightmare, not only in terms of compliance, if you are a small business operator, but also the nightmare of having to pay out hundreds and perhaps thousands of dollars in additional tax every year.
I make an appeal to my hon. friend, the member for Kingston and the Islands to wander down the hallway, talk to some of his Liberal pals in the Senate and ask them to do what they do in the House, and say: "If we are going to say as a political party that we oppose the GST, surely to goodness you folks in there should now vote against it".
I encourage my hon. friend to do just that. While it is there, let's take advantage of this group. However, it seems like those appeals are going in one ear and out the other, as far as the Senators are concerned, because they do not seem to be taking the opportunity to defeat the GST very seriously.
June 11, 1990

them out of their misery. At the moment, they do have the authority.
