speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
I am sure the Speaker will feel a warm sentiment towards that appointment.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to participate in this debate briefly, as I did at second reading, and make it clear that the Liberal caucus will be voting against this measure. We will, as we have all along this process, keep telling

June 11, 1990
Government Orders
the government how the proposal before the House is negative and bad.
Mr. Speaker, in my opening comments I would like explain that the purpose of Bill C-69 is to restrain the government's public spending by a two-year freeze on federal transfers to the provinces under Established Programs Financing, including post-secondary education and health care.
Second, this bill proposes to cap federal transfers under the Canada Assistance Plan to Ontario, British Columbia and Alberta at 5 per cent for the next two years.
Third, Bill C-69 proposes to eliminate the Canadian Exploration Incentive Program and finally, it proposes a two-year freeze on Public Utilities Income Tax Transfers to the provinces.
Mr. Speaker, two aspects of particular interest to me are of course Established Programs Financing which has a direct impact on Canadians because it affects health care and postsecondary education, and the Canada Assistance Plan which is also very important to Canadians because it plan helps families or individuals facing serious problems due to poverty to cope with these problems.
Mr. Speaker, cutbacks in transfers to the provinces for post-secondary education and health care-in fact, the three provinces that are most severely affected are Alberta, British Columbia and my own province Ontario-will force these provinces to accept a reduction in services, reduction in service quality or a reduction in access to these services, or if the provinces so decide, they will have to substantially increase the provincial tax burden of each resident. According to the figures I have before me, in the three provinces in question, the tax bill for each citizen will increase $576 during the next five years.
This is the third time, Mr. Speaker, that this government has attacked Established Programs Financing since 1986. All told, total cutbacks in program financing between 1986-87 and 1994-95 will reach the astronomical figure of $31.1 billion, as follows: $22.2 billion which should have gone to health care and $8.9 billion to higher education.
Were the provinces to choose not to raise their taxes they would have to shift these reductions on to hospitals-as I said earlier, fewer services, fewer beds, limit on costly surgery-or to students who will be expected to pay higher tuition fees in exchange for the privilege of attending overcrowded lectures and working with outmoded equipment which badly need to be replaced. The ultimate effect of all this will be lower post-secondary education quality throughout the country.
Mr. Speaker, let me remind you of a statement made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in March 1982. The Minister of Finance said to the House, and I quote his very words: "Let us not make hospitals, universities and colleges a battleground between the federal government and the provincial governments. Let us solve those problems outside of that arena".
That is what he said barely eight years ago, Mr. Speaker, but today the same Minister of Finance has changed his mind, as he often does, and imposes restrictive measures on universities and hospitals in spite of the fact that he once stated that we should not shift the fiscal burden on to these two services.
With respect to the Canada Assistance Plan, the lower benefits to poorer people in the provinces of Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia fly in the face of this government's commitment to help, and I quote, to help people in need".
Mr. Speaker, I should think that poor people in Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia are just as poor as other poor people who live in Quebec, Manitoba or Nova Scotia. Being poor is a sad situation, but we do have poor people in Ottawa-Vanier. Mr. Speaker, who will tell me that a poor man in Ottawa-Vanier does not have the right to the same kind of attention and the same kind of assistance as everybody else to meet his own needs? Who will argue that a poor man in Ottawa-Vanier is not as poor as a poor man in Nova Scotia or Quebec?
Mr. Speaker, I find this formula totally unacceptable and I object to it, and others have decided to take the matter to court. Hon. members would know that a province has gone to court to argue about the constitutionality of Bill C-69. I wish it good luck, Mr. Speaker, because this measure has been introduced by a government which is running out of steam, which is discouraging and discouraged, and which may well need help from
June 11, 1990

the courts to get back on course and steer the country properly.
As for mining exploration, I will let other colleagues speak to this issue because for the time being it does not seriously concern my constituents.
I would like to make a few remarks about two or three important aspects of education. In my riding, Mr. Speaker, are the University of Ottawa; a community college, Algonquin College; and a French-language college that is being set up. Besides suffering from the federal government's transfer payment cuts since 1986, these three institutions have been the target of many government policies. In addition to the extra costs for health insurance in Ontario, the University of Ottawa, which is entirely in my riding, will be hard hit by the new goods and services tax. I suggest that hon. members give a little thought to the impact this goods and services tax will have on university administrations. The Unemployment Insurance Act, Mr. Speaker, will cost them more; for example, for the University of Ottawa alone it will cost $400,000 more a year. With the freeze in fiscal transfers, we have reason to fear that the University of Ottawa will have to spend more time claiming the funds it needs than being concerned about an effective teaching program. That worries me, Mr. Speaker. When the administrators tell me that they spend more time asking for money and claiming their due, it is disturbing.
We listen to the students, Mr. Speaker. Here is what the Student Federation of the University of Ottawa said recently when it spoke against the freeze in transfer payments, and I know these students. It considers the freeze a major loss for post-secondary education. Marc Molgat, the vice-president for external affairs of the federation, said, "Post-secondary education is a right and an investment in our country's social and economic development." He thinks it is unfair of the federal government not to require that the provinces spend what they receive or not to spend fixed amounts on education. The federation is understandably opposed to any increase in tuition fees charged to students.
Mr. Speaker, I have tabled in this House petitions signed by hundreds and thousands of students in my
Government Orders
riding who are worried about the condition of their institutions. I will read some of the complaints contained in their petitions: overcrowded lecture halls, deteriorating lab equipment, lock of library resources, high student-teacher ratio, elimination of certain courses, deteriorating buildings and facilities. All this is true. It is typical today of Canada's post-secondary education system. This is not just in Ottawa. It is like that across the country.
I shall continue: native students, the handicapped and other students who are socially and economically disadvantaged are under-represented at the post-secondary level. We all know that. These are the consequences of 12 years of declining financing per student since the present legislation on post-secondary financing was passed in 1977.
Mr. Speaker, this is still going on today. These students reject injustice, soaring tuition fees and other costs that today are a consequence of the deteriorating quality of our post-secondary education system. These students have sounded the alarm. They want us to understand, as Canadians, that this neglect on the part of the government will cost us dearly in that we will have to change our policy towards these post-secondary institutions and perhaps loosen the purse strings a bit.
When it appeared before the finance committee on May 16 this year, the Canadian Federation of Students protested these new measures and said it doubted the federal government's commitment to quality and fully accessible post-secondary education. I quote the federation: "Regardless of these pre-election commitments, the Conservative Party has repeatedly reduced the rate of growth of transfer payments for post-secondary education." The chairperson of the federation, Jane Arnold, stated, and I quote: "In constant dollars, the cuts to post-secondary education are even more drastic when consideration is given to the rise in course costs and educational materials. In addition, tuition has doubled at most institutions in the last 10 years. The crisis in education funding means larger classes, decreased resources for research, inadequate library facilities and deteriorating institutions."

June 11, 1990
Government Orders

For members of the House who represent universities and post-secondary institutions as I do, it is an important debate on the quality of education and the access to education.
I was reviewing my notes and looking at the history of EPF transfers. It is disquieting. It is worrisome to me to see post-secondary education and research in those institutions going down, and to see the access to those institutions being restricted to those who can afford to pay. I find that difficult to accept in my Canada, because I was brought up in that period of time when one went to university if one's father and mother had the money to pay. I thought we got rid of that. I thought that now post-secondary education was available to all those who met the basic requirements of admission to the institutions.
Every day I meet young people who say to me: "I cannot go to university because I cannot afford it." I thought we had addressed that problem. I guess we still have a long way to go before we have paid justice to that issue.

Mr. Speaker, I remember the Nielsen Report. I do not know if hon. members will remember it. But this statement that I am going to read is more disturbing than anything I have read so far. The Nielsen Report was prepared by the government, by their Deputy Prime Minister and a committee or task force charged with examining education and research programs. The Nielsen Report says that no longer contributing to the basic funding of post-secondary educational institutions would be justified because the Constitution gives the federal government no specific role in this field.
Mr. Speaker, that is the way the Conservative government is going. According to Statistics Canada, the federal government spent $6.7 billion for education and training, an increase of 1.8 per cent compared to a 3.6 per cent increase for total government spending. In 1975, 7.3 per cent of federal government spending was for education, whereas in 1988, it was only 6.7 per cent. Although the number of students attending post-secondary institutions rose 4.4 per cent between 1985 and 1989, government spending for education rose by 2.3 per
cent (annually) compared to a 4.2 per cent (annual) increase for the consumer price index.
Before slashing the spending of higher education institutions by cutting transfer payments to the provinces, the federal government, together with the provinces, should draw up a specific plan setting forth a coherent policy covering the administrative and financial responsibilities for post-secondary education.

I know I only have a few minutes and I want to address the other very important question, health care.
I received a letter from a constituent of mine, Dr. Robert Walker, and I want to read one paragraph of that letter because it touches on the subject matter. Dr. Walker stated: "I am writing as a constituent and, in particular, as a family physician who works daily with economically disadvantaged families and individuals in an Ottawa community health centre. My concern is the ceiling placed on the Canada Assistance Plan moneys for Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia in the recent federal budget. I want to relate my strong disapproval of this decision. As it so adversely affects the lives of many of my patients, I request that you direct efforts to ensure that the proposed ceiling on federal dollars directed to the provinces for people in need be deleted from Bill C-69."
Dr. Walker goes on to explain that a large percentage of patients are either low-income or welfare recipients. Dr. Walker makes the case that these people need our assistance, need our help, and that Bill C-69 does not address the problems of those people.
Indeed, by voting against this bill, I will try to register in the name of all my constituents, a strong vote of protest against the government.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to compliment my colleague, the hon. member from Ottawa-Vanier, and to say that, as a member from another city where the universities are an integral and vital part of the life of our city, I was particularly taken by his comments with regard to what the cutbacks in funding in this bill will do to our universities.
I would like to ask the hon. member if he has had much dealing with the students, in particular, with regard to the increases in tuition fees. I know it is not quite the same in the province of Ontario as in the province of Nova Scotia. The situation that is becoming more and more crucial in Nova Scotia is that as the
June 11, 1990

universities have to cut back, the tuition fees go up and the university students cannot any longer possibly earn the money to supplement student loans or find other sources of income to pay for their university tuition. Even if the student finds a job, it is just not possible to earn enough in one summer to supplement whatever he or she may have to pay tuition fees.
I am wondering if this particular problem exists in the Ottawa area as well.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the member for Halifax for her question. It is an important question because constitutionally, education is a provincial matter. We have a variety of programs in certain provinces so that access to universities is nearly a right, whereas in other provinces the access to universities is pretty near impossible.
I have some press clippings here from the Federation of Canadian Students which explains the lack of equality of access to post-secondary education across this country and how difficult it is to pursue a career with university training today unless one can go into post-graduate studies or, for that matter, graduate studies.
I know for a fact that in my riding many students planning to go into the sciences, arts or other faculties at the University of Ottawa cannot because of financial difficulties. Students must pay the academic fee that is required plus cope with the expenditures that they have living outside their homes.
We must never forget that every community, hamlet, village and every town of this country must have access to post-secondary education. We must have a program that is designed to give everybody, wherever he lives, a chance on an equal basis, to have access to not only the post-secondary education which he or she chooses, but the financing allowed.
We have some good programs. We have some good student loan programs, but we have to think up new theories and new good programs to give our young
Government Orders
people wherever they live in this country, a chance for a post-secondary education.

Mr. Speaker, I too am very pleased to have an opportunity to speak again to Bill C-69. I feel that it is very important to speak, because this bill strikes at the very heart of what it is to be a Canadian.
If you ask a Canadian to define a Canadian, probably the initial reaction may well be that we are different and that we are special. But what is that difference? As Canadians, we are forever wrestling with defining that difference. We are seemingly wrestling with our identity, trying to define just exactly what it means to be a Canadian.
We know that we are different from our southern neighbours, yet we cannot always define what those differences are. Yet we are all tremendously proud to be Canadian.
Upon a closer look, there are many differences between our two nations, the most obvious being the social programs that we have in Canada. Canadians pride themselves in the manner in which they take care of their children, the poor, the elderly and the sick.
We take extra special care to make sure that all Canadians, regardless of their social, economic, cultural or linguistic backgrounds, are given every opportunity to succeed and lead a successful, satisfying and productive life. Canadians have always held on to these values as being distinctively Canadian.
We have always placed more emphasis on our government's role in these areas. The present government seems intent on becoming more American than on maintaining our sovereignty and programs that are essential to the Canadian value system. It seems intent on changing our value system and I say that that is wrong.
Bill C-69 cuts at the very heart of the Canadian value system. It sets a new agenda on how we spend money on post-secondary education, health care, and on assistance to the needy in this country. In 1982 the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre rose in his place in the House and declared that any cuts to Established Programs Financing: "could have disastrous effects on the universities and on the colleges, on the hospital funding and on the

June 11, 1990
Government Orders
operation of hospitals. Let us not make hospitals, universities and colleges a battleground between the federal government and the provincial governments. Let us solve those problems not on the backs of hospitals and universities; let us solve those problems outside of that arena."
That quote was from the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre in 1982. Had I been a member of this House at that time and on that day, and had I been sitting in this House I probably would have applauded that member of Parliament.
Since then, we know that he is on the government side of the House and has become the Minister of Finance. My only comment to him at this time is a great big resounding, "Boo."
Everyday Canadians are becoming less tolerant of the hypocrisy of the government. In particular, the Minister of Finance is one whose words are often radically different than his actions. If we look at the proposed goods and services tax, there are so many broken promises that I am now embarrassed for the minister. I wonder how he could go back on so many of his promises, as he has, and still look at himself in the mirror.
Look at the government's promises on child care, environment, unemployment, Atlantic fisheries and income tax. There are all kinds of examples. We can talk about what we read today on the front page of our local newspaper, The Ottawa Citizen. It states that while the government asks Canadians to tighten their belts, federal bosses received bonuses up to 25 per cent. Some of these bonuses work out to as much as $100,000. That is absolutely disgraceful.
Again, let me talk about what Bill C-69 will do to post-secondary education. I have said in this House in the past that funding for post-secondary education should not be seen as an expenditure. It is an investment in our young people and an investment in Canada's future. Bill C-69 is set to act upon the 1990 budget, which in effect freezes any growth in federal funding for post-secondary education.
The EPF helps the provinces to carry out their responsibilities with respect to health care and post-secondary education. Since the federal government provides equal per capital financial assistance to all
provinces, the freeze means that the payments will grow only with the population increase of each province, or about 1 per cent nationally. The impact of the EPF cuts on federal transfers to the provinces will amount to about $3.1 billion over five years. When coupled with previous EPF reductions since 1983, the cumulative effect of the cuts is obvious and amounts to $8.9 billion.
The cumulative reduction in federal contributions from the 1986-87 to 1994-95 fiscal year amounts to an incredible $31.1 billion. All these cuts, coupled with the government's recently imposed 3 per cent fee on student loans will increase the cost of post-secondary education to all students, particularly to those who can least afford it.
Federal spending on education has increased at an average annual rate of 2.3 per cent since 1985, while the consumer price index has averaged 4.2 per cent per year. This shows that, despite its rhetoric, the present government is doing very little for education in this country. The government should be encouraging students to participate in higher education, instead of slashing its affordability. Ironically, early last month, the junior science minister complained that a lack of skilled scientists and engineers threatens the ability of Canadian industiy to compete in the world. He pointed out that Canada has only 90 scientists and researchers for every 100,000 people compared with 280 per 100,000 in the United States and 240 for 100,000 in Japan.
While his complaints are justified, his accusations as to who is to blame or who is at fault are not. He puts the blame squarely on the backs of Canadian business, without mentioning the inaction of his own government.
While it is true that less than 3 per cent of Canadian companies are involved in R and D on any scale, the government must begin to accept its vital role in this important area. This is clearly not being done. Despite repeated promises by the Prime Minister to double the amount of money Canada spends on research and development, statistics indicate that Canada's percentage of R and D spending has actually decreased.
Recently in Edmonton the minister rejected a key recommendation for a major R and D funding boost from 10 provincial and two national science and technology advisory councils.
June 11, 1990

Canada has a negative trade balance and a growing trade deficit in every single sector of the advanced technology industry. According to Dr. Fraser Mustard, President of the Canadian Institute for Advanced Research, unless the Canadian scientific community receives more money, "we might not be a trading nation, we might be a fading nation".
The government is just standing by and letting our high tech sector become more and more of a branch plant economy. Increasingly, companies specializing in R and D, such as Lumonics, are being sold to foreign interests. If we look at what happened to Leigh Instruments as an example of the type of commitment foreign interests have for our workers, we are in big trouble. Dr. Polanyi, a Canadian Nobel Prize winning scientist advises Canadian scientists to go to the United States, which would result in a terrible brain drain if our brilliant young minds are forced to leave Canada for higher prospects elsewhere.
We need our scientists and researchers to remain in Canada. We need our scientific and technologic advances and potential to remain in Canadian hands if we wish to have long-term prosperity. It is the responsibility of the government to work with business to ensure this happens. Cutting back EPF transfers to the provinces does not go in that direction. It is a step backward.
The cuts to EPF transfers will also have a detrimental effect on health care here in Canada. The President of the Canadian Hospital Association, Mrs. Carol Clemen-hagen, told the Standing Committee on Finance that:
- prior to the February 20 budget, the CHA calculated that the cumulative loss the provinces have already experienced from 1986-87 to 1989-90 because of 1he 2 per cent reduction in EPF growth was $2.6 billion, and the projected cumulative loss to the provinces from 1990-91 to 1995-96 because of the combined 3 per cent reduction in EPF growth is $19.4 billion.
Reductions in the EPF transfers challenge provincial governments either to reduce health care and post-secondary education budgets or to increase taxes. We believe a national framework, a stable and adequate EPF funding is a prerequisite to achieving health goals. In the case of health manpower, cuts to EPF threaten both the health system in which health professionals work and the educational system in which they were trained.
Let us hope that the government will realize before we have gone too far down the road to turn back, that by breaking the commitment to a vital social program, the government is breaking a long-standing Canadian tradi-
Government Orders
tion of caring for the sick. This bill lashes out at that fundamental Canadian belief. This is appalling.
Now I would like to turn to the cuts to the Canada Assistance Plan, which are cuts to the poorest in the provinces of Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia. The poor in Alberta, B.C. and Ontario are just as poor as the poor in the other provinces. It is my belief that the cuts to CAP contradict the government's commitment to come to the aid of those who are in need.
As I outlined at the second reading of this bill, under CAP the federal and provincial governments share equally in the cost of welfare payments and basic necessities such as food, shelter, clothing and dental care for the poor, and essential services for the disabled.
This is the first time in the history of the program that CAP has been limited. It is a shame. While the government has raised taxes 32 times since it took office and collects $48 billion more today than it did five years ago, I find it incredible that it has cut this essential program. It claims that it is cutting these things in the name of deficit reduction, but I believe that most Canadians feel that certain things are essential, and that health care is one of those things.
Cutting CAP will force the provinces either to raise taxes or more poor will become even poorer with no hope.
Finally, the government has also frozen public utilities income tax transfers over the next two years. These programs provide for over 95 per cent of the federal income tax collected from certain privately owned electric and gas utilities. The program was initiated in order to put private electric and gas companies which pay federal tax on an equal footing with Crown corporations in the resource sector which do not pay tax.
I firmly believe that Canadian opportunities must be fundamental to our way of life. They have been in the past and will continue to be in the future, especially when the present government is replaced by a Liberal government in two or three years.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, the present government has attempted to tear at the very heart of what it is to be Canadian and I firmly believe that Canadians will, nevertheless, maintain those same values. Canadians will stand up and overcome the hypocrisy of this present government. As I said at second reading, this government has lost all sense of propriety and this is a

June 11, 1990
Government Orders
reflection of the extreme limits to which it will go to force its will on the people.

Mr. Speaker, I have looked at Bill C-69 and gone over the remarks of the Minister of State for Finance in first introducing this bill. Part of the difficulty I have had over the last 18 months that I have been in Parliament is my difficulty with the plan or the concept that this government seems to be heading toward. I looked at the remarks of the minister for some consolation in this particular area. I would like to just pull out some of the remarks that he talked about in referring to this bill.
The minister talked talks about the measures in this bill "having a clear goal, controlling inflation, and securing steady non-inflationary economic growth in Canada". He went on to say "that attaining this goal will lead to a bright economic future that, of course, we all want for this country". We have no argument with a bright economic future.
He went on to say that "the restraint measures as set out in this bill are part of the government's consistent comprehensive plan to ensure that Canadians benefit from a standard of living and a quality of life that is second to none". Once again, it is a goal that certainly we in Canada would like to strive toward. Later he goes on to say "this bill takes a further step along the path we have been following since 1984". I think that is the crux of the matter right there.
It is this path that this government has been following since 1984 and more and more seems to be leading Canada into a polarity; a polarity of economic regions, a polarity of economic roots and a polarity of individuals, some who are poor and some who are rich. More and more the legislation that we have seen put before the House of Commons has been an attack on middle income groups and the poor in this country.
Once again, as we look through Bill C-69, I suggest that this once more is an attack on that which the minister said we were striving toward, an attack on economic equality for the regions and for the individuals of Canada.
I point to an article in The Toronto Star, February 26, 1990. It is an article on social policy by Leonard Shifrin and I quote from it:
The two-year freeze on federal contributions to the provinces for health and post-secondary education affects everyone. Freezing contributions for legal aid and cutting funds for social housing aims directly at the poor.
And so does the ceiling on Canada Assistance Plan (CAP) contributions to Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia, because CAP is the funding program for welfare payments and services to the poor.
It points out in that article that all across the political spectrum, here in Ontario and in the rest of Canada, we have been appalled to learn that children are the largest group on welfare and the chief victims to the rules that keep mother-led families dependent on it. Once again, I point out through these quotes that what we have seen in the capping of the Canada Assistance Plan is a direct attack on the poor.
I wonder about the methods that have been used in this process, the process in the UI bill, in the clawback legislation and in the goods and service tax, of setting specific deadlines and then pushing to try to meet those deadlines. When looking at some of the history of this, I looked at the twenty-seventh annual premiers conference in Edmonton, Alberta, in August 1986, and what the provincial premiers saw when they looked at the Canada Assistance Plan and Established Programs Financing.
I want to quote from various sections of that conference to make the point that what we have seen is a breaking down of the consultative process between the government and the opposition, the government and the provinces, the government and the regions and the government and groups that will be affected by the legislation that they bring in. They quote, first of all, from the federal-provincial agreements section of the communique which states: "Premiers recognize that federal-provincial agreements and arrangements have become an important instrument of government. They expressed concern that unilateral changes to these agreements and arrangements are very disruptive".
Later, under tax reform, it states: "The premiers stressed that tax reform must not be used by the federal government as an excuse to erode provincial health and
June 11, 1990

post-secondary education support by further cutbacks and transfer payments. The process of tax reform must be open to consultation among all Canadians. The premiers emphasized the need for federal-provincial consultation, co-operation and consensus building".
What we see in this bill is a breakdown of that system. There have apparently been very few consultations. I recognize that the premier of the province of British Columbia, in his zeal to advise the federal government on how to manage its financial problems, suggested that it cut the Established Programs Financing and the transfer payments from the federal to the provincial government by up to 15 per cent, and cries when that has been done. That is not what we in British Columbia have been looking for. We have been looking for a proper priorization and a proper consultation process as to where some of these cuts, if they are needed, should take place.
The committee went through hearings in a very short time span, hearing some groups and refusing others the opportunity of appearing before the committee. Once again, the consultative process has broken down. The federal government has not consulted with the premiers, the provinces, the medical profession, the post-secondary education institutions or the poverty groups in trying to come up with some fair and equitable way for the future. Let me just touch briefly for those in the riding of Okanagan-Similkameen-Merritt on exactly what this bill is and what it attacks. The Established Programs Financing is the method by which the federal government transfers to the provinces funding for such things as post-secondary education and health. It is put into the general provincial coffers to be used primarily for health and education, but not necessarily in that manner. The Canada Assistance Plan is to be used for welfare payments, social assistance, counselling and other things dealing with the social assistance and welfare areas.
Having said that, I would like to turn directly to the Established Programs Financing and look at how this will affect, in my province, things like hospitals and universities. Specifically, I fear, in looking at the cutbacks in these areas, and this fear has been set out by some of the university groups which have appeared before the committee, that we are looking at a move toward the gradual privatization of our universities. More and more, funding is being cut out from our post-secondary education units
Government Orders
and more and more they are having to turn to the private sector to try to get their funding.
I have a fear of that move toward privatization because, as I said in my introductory remarks, this polarization we have seen, a polarization toward the poor getting poorer and the rich getting richer, is going to translate into the area of higher education. Access through privatization will be cut off, the cost will increase for tuition and, therefore, we are again going to set aside a whole group in our society who will be unable to attend university. We therefore put down those most in need of the assistance.
We have a problem within the Okanagan and Similkameen regions in that we have a very high percentage of seniors in those regions, in some cases triple the national average of 11 per cent. One of the larger hospitals in the area, the Penticton Regional Hospital, has done a paper that looks at age-related cost in their particular facility. The Penticton Regional Hospital is a 200-bed acute care referral hospital for the south Okanagan and the Similkameen regions and serves a population base of approximately 65,000 people. In reviewing some of the costs that they have added, over and above other areas within the province of British Columbia alone, they note that the hospital costs for our seniors is substantially higher. I point particularly to the populations in the towns, for instance, like Keremeos, where over 34 per cent of the residents of that community are over 65 years of age. Oliver is pushing 35 per cent of the population over 65 years of age, Osoyoos is in the area of 33 per cent, and it goes on.
This study used 1981 figures which are now substantially out of date and it states that in the over-all area it was almost 20 per cent at that time in 1981. Those figures have been shown, in a recent study, to be substantially lower. But the added costs in that area are for seniors, who have been shown to have additional hospital care costs, because of the very nature of the time of their life. The cuts in these particular programs are again attacking one area of our society.
We know that recently in the communities of Grand Forks, Merritt, Kelowna, and Oliver residents have gone through the traumatic experience of having one of their number not able to get adequate health care, in that they required transplants or specific operations to the heart or other parts of the body. They were not able to get that care without having their names placed first on long

Government Orders
waiting lists. By the time their names were at the top of these long waiting lists it was too late; they had already died. That is the type of thing that I am pointing to.
The nurses have made the situation clear in some of their submissions. They have said: "Pressure is growing to get rid of the medicare system Canadians know and cherish". federal government support. I am wondering whether my friend has a concern in that area.

Mr. Speaker, I do not think there is any doubt about it. As we look at what has happened over the last six years in particular we have seen a major attack on our health care system and on our universal programs.

to amend certain statutes to enable restraint of government expenditures.
I spoke before on this bill during the second reading stage. At that time I explained to the House how poorly this government managed its affairs in the cancellation of the CEIP, the Canadian Exploration Incentives Program. The same thing happened with regard to CFB Sum-merside. This government announced its closure in the budget of April 1989 without any consultation with the people of Prince Edward Island, and obviously without any thought or planning for what would happen to Summerside and the entire area.
The role of government has always been managing the present while planning and organizing for the future. I grant that there are a number of times and situations when government cannot plan, but the goal and certainly the intention of government should always be to plan ahead.
Obviously this government is not planning ahead. Here we have another piece of legislation, Bill C-69, which is one more example of the government's lack of planning.
Within the title of this bill we see the words "enable restraint". Canadians want to see restraint take place but certainly not at a cost to the future development of the country.
Islanders also want restraint. They want to help and do their fair share in tackling the tremendous deficit that we have in this country, but, again, they do not want to do it at the expense of important policy programs such as health and education.
The government's financial plan for 1990-91 contains several measures which will cost the province of Prince Edward Island millions of dollars. The largest cut of course comes in the form of reduced transfer payments for education and health. Certainly we on Prince Edward Island, all Islanders, feel that education and health are top priorities. Transfer payments for education enable our young men and women to get a university or college

education, remain on the Island, and put their skills to work for the province.
This helps Prince Edward Island develop as a province, makes it more self-sufficient and of course less dependent on the federal government, but here before us we have a piece of legislation, Bill C-69, which really works in the opposite direction. It would reduce federal spending, money that goes into post-secondary education. Thus it is not contributing to the development of the future of our youth and tomorrow's leaders.
Canadians are also very proud of their health system, and rightly so. We have one of the best health care systems in the world. It is certainly a system that we do not want to lose. Yet this legislation, Bill C-69, means that Prince Edward Island will receive less money for health.
As I just mentioned, Prince Edward Islanders put great emphasis on education and health care, but we are disturbed by the record of this government. Since the Tory government came to power in 1984 it has on three separate occasions-not just one, but three separate occasions-reduced the amount of transfer payments to the provinces for medicare, hospital services, and education.

Now we have before us Bill C-69 with which the government wants to freeze the payments. The impact of all these cuts will mean a loss of $155 million to my province up to the year 1995.
It is plain to see that this government is simply eroding the post-education system across our country. To put things in a political perspective, the Prime Minister promised before the 1984 election: "We are committed to sustaining the current federal financial commitment. We believe that financing post-secondary education is an important priority for both levels of government".

That is what the Prime Minister said before the election in 1984, but actions speak louder than words. The actions of this government have certainly not been to carry through on that commitment. I say that because we have had on three occasions transfer payments cut or reduced. This is the money that goes to the provinces to pay for health, hospitals and education.
The government has now certainly abandoned the commitment that the Prime Minister talked about, as we see in this legislation before us, and as we have seen in previous legislation. Clearly, this government does not know how to determine policy in view of the future of this country.
I had the opportunity to be a member of the legislative committee which studied this bill on the day the committee heard representatives of the Canadian Federation of Students who came before the committee to tell us what they thought of this legislation. I want to quote one sentence from their brief.
The Federation shares the opinion of many in the educational
community that Bill C-69 is one of a series of cutbacks which have
resulted in the serious underfunding of our post-secondary education
system.
They went on to indicate to us in their brief just how Bill C-69 will affect the education system. They indicated to us the negative impact that will be felt across this country in our universities and colleges.
The funding of universities and colleges is not the only way that students are being hit by this government. This government has also failed to update the student loan system which has not kept up with inflation and which discriminates against part-time students.
A student advisory group was set up to provide the government with input on these student aid matters. That group was in existence for over two years before the minister finally decided to meet with it to get its input. I understand that meeting took place in March. It was a very short meeting. The students feel that that meeting was to no avail.
So what we have is a government that is really continuing to ignore the concerns of students. That seems to be the story of this government. It really fails to consult with the people who are going to be affected by these decisions.
The same thing happened with the decision to close CFB Summerside. As I mentioned earlier, the government announced this decision in its budget of 1989. Out of the blue the government announced that it was going to close CFB Summerside.
There had been no consultation with Islanders, with the people who would be affected by this decision. Obviously, there was no planning whatsoever as to what was going to happen to the economy of Summerside, Prince Edward Island after the base closed. In fact, the lack of forethought put into this dramatic decision is really frightening.
The closure of CFB Summerside will mean the loss of 1,300 jobs. The effect of this announcement was to put the economy of that whole area on hold. It left the people uncertain about their future.
I would like to outline very briefly the order of events for my colleagues here in the House today so that they have a good understanding of how the people of Summerside and area have been treated by this government since the announcement of that decision in the budget of 1989.
The announcement was made public on April 27 of that year. For an entire year the people of Summerside and the surrounding area were left in limbo, not knowing what was in store for them. The people who work at the base did not know. They still do not know whether they are going to have jobs. They do not know whether they should try to sell their houses, move to Tbronto or elsewhere to try and find a job. That still has not been cleared up.
What the federal government did in July is set up a federal task force which was headed by the Minister of Employment and Immigration. That task force was to look into the possibilities for CFB Summerside.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration visited the Island at the end of October. That was three months after the task force had been set up, and six months after the announcement that this base was going to be closed.
Another six months went by, until March 27 of this year, when the Minister of Employment and Immigration visited Summerside and announced that a development corporation would be established to take on the assets of CFB Summerside. That meant that interim

management would be appointed for the corporation to negotiate with any prospective tenants between now and 1992 when the base is to officially close.
One of the questions that Islanders are now asking is why this interim management for the corporation has not been appointed. Has it been appointed, but simply not been announced? It has been three months since the announcement. Yet we on Prince Edward Island have heard nothing.
Here again it seems the government has left everyone in limbo. It appears that there is no plan ahead at all.
The people in Summerside and area are really frustrated with this whole process. The chairman of the crisis centre in Summerside, which has been looking after the needs of those affected by the decision to close the base, said just this past weekend: "We are frustrated. As every day passes without interim management in place time is wasted. It is time that could have been spent in attracting tenants to the facility. Since my time is running out, I would like to end my comments by saying that certainly Prince Edward Island wants to participate in the Confederation of Canada. We know that that means sharing the responsibilities of deficits as well as surpluses. We are certainly willing to

do our fair share, but this government's economic policies go far beyond being fair and equitable.
What we have is a transfer of the deficit of the federal government to the provinces. It is certainly a burden which will erode the economy of my province and the quality of life in Prince Edward Island.

have a question, Mr. Speaker.

is coming in January of 1991. The average person just cannot afford to pay any more taxes.
We come to the third option of the provincial government and, as my hon. friend alluded to, that is taking money from other departments and putting it into health and education in order to provide the same quality of service in those two areas. speakeroldname: Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands- Canso):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to participate in this debate on Bill C-69,1 would like to draw the attention of the House to a principle that goes back to the report of the Rowell-Sirois Commission of the 1930s. It has become so fundamental to the design of the Canadian federation that, in 1982, it was expressed directly in the
Constitution. That is the principle that I would term as regional equity. It is commitment of Canadians living in more well-off provinces or regions to share their resources with less well-off regions, so that the latter may, as a minimum, enjoy the same or similar basic levels of public service without, I might add, being obliged to bear an undue burden of taxes.
It was the recognition in the early years of this century that a growing imbalance had occurred in the fiscal capacity of different provinces and regions that led to the formation of the Rowell-Sirois Commission. It was that commission's far-seeing report that began the establishment of the framework of federal-provincial fiscal arrangements that exist today.
The principle that all provinces should be able to provide their citizens with comparable levels of public services at comparable levels of taxes is the basis for the equalization payments system worked out since the 1950s. It has been supplemented by the combination of shared-cost programs and tax transfer programs, some of which were consolidated in the late seventies under the Established Programs Financing and which apply to federal transfers for health and post-secondary education, as well as the whole framework of other cost-shared programs which exist in Canada today.
This framework was supplemented in the 1960s by active programs to limit and ultimately to eliminate the problem of regional disparities, the widening of the gap in income opportunities across various regions of the country. These positive, progressive programs were introduced by Liberal governments over the years.
It is these programs and this framework of federal-provincial arrangements that are being undermined, that are under attack by this Tory government and have been since it took office in 1984. It is these same programs and the underlying principles that are under attack with Bill C-69.
One of the four components of Bill C-69, the one with the greatest fiscal impact, is the one that would alter the formula for federal payments to provinces under the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements and Federal Post-secondary Education and Health Contributions Act.
June 11, 1990

This component, which is expressed in clauses 5 and 6 of this bill, would freeze federal transfer payments to the provinces under Established Programs Financing for the next two years. With costs rising elsewhere, this actually translates into an effective cut in federal transfers to provincial governments.
In effect, along with those Canadians who, unlike its corporate friends, cannot escape this government's tax net, provincial governments are being asked to bear the burden of the belated preoccupation of the Minister of Finance with deficit reduction.
In 1990 and 1991, the total amount of these cuts across Canada will be in the order of $869 million. For the full five-year period the amount will be more than $7.3 billion. The effect of these measures on the fiscal capacity in particular of less well off provinces which the system was designed to help is being compounded by the government's high interest rate policies and the damper that this is causing on local economic activity, not to mention municipal and provincial borrowing charges.
Of course, Canadians are already bracing themselves for the impact of the GST which will be an unprecedented tax grab by the government.
The effects of cutbacks in Established Program Financing this year and in previous years has already meant provincial cutbacks in services and increases in taxes and charges to residents who can least afford to pay.
Let us take my province of Nova Scotia as an example. In his budget, released on Friday, April 27, the finance minister of Nova Scotia, Mr. Greg Kerr, reported that federal funding cutbacks for health and post-secondary education for 1990-91, alone, would cost the province of Nova Scotia $140 million.
Provincial revenues from this category which comprise about 9.3 per cent of total provincial revenues are actually expected to drop in absolute terms down from $377 million for 1988-89 to $350 million for 1990-91. Even if the provincial finance minister was a prudent manager of the provincial treasury, a drop of that magnitude in these difficult times would be tough to absorb without either losses in basic services or increases in taxes.
As we in Nova Scotia know, prudent management of provincial finances has not been a trademark of the Tory government of Nova Scotia. These are lessons it may
Government Orders
well have imparted on the federal Tory government in Ottawa since it took office.
Nova Scotia has experienced, as a result of that budget, both an increase in taxes and a reduction in services. For example, children in Nova Scotia will now be charged an additional $3 fee for dental services and seniors will now be expected to pay fees for prescription drugs under the Nova Scotia Pharmacare Plan. These are costs the Nova Scotia government is now imposing indirectly on Nova Scotians as a result of cutbacks by the federal government in its transfers to that province.
Of particular concern in my riding of Cape Breton- Highlands-Canso is the upheaval these changes have produced in the secondary education system, particularly in rural Nova Scotia. The government of Nova Scotia has cut back on funds to municipalities and schools boards across the province with the result that schools in those areas already hard hit, which are strained to the limit, over-crowded and have not received capital funds over the years, are now being asked to bear an additional strain. The result is an attitude on the part of parents, students and teachers that enough is enough. There have been demonstrations of outrage at the cutbacks to education in communities across Cape Breton-Highlands-Canso and the province of Nova Scotia.
These cuts have also produced additional tensions in the school system. In Richmond County, parents and teachers are being asked to choose either closing schools and double-grading students or busing young students long distances to school.
In other parts of the province there is a conflict emerging between French and English classes. French immersion programs and English classes are competing for dwindling funds with the result that tensions arise between students where French immersion courses are offered.
The numbers of teachers have been cut and in some cases schools have been reduced or closed. All this is an indirect result of cutbacks by the federal government in its transfer programs. The result is additional tensions in rural parts of Nova Scotia.
These cuts have also had an effect on post-secondary education. Tuition fees in Nova Scotia are already among the highest in the country. These cutbacks by the federal government will put additional burden on our universities. As my colleague mentioned earlier, student loans

have not kept up with the escalating costs of attending university and therefore students face more difficulty attending university.

These are the kinds of direct impacts which Bill C-69 is having and will continue to have on federal, provincial and municipal services, on our education system, and on our health system across the country, particularly in areas in which the fiscal capacity, the tax base, the capacity of provinces to bear the burden of these increases is the smallest. As a result, provinces like Nova Scotia increasingly are being asked to tighten their belts and cut back on basic services which we in Canada have come to expect as a kind of right of citizenship in this country, in this day and age.
In conclusion, I want to say that I am personally opposed to this legislation, to its thrust and to the implications which these cutbacks will have, particularly in those parts of the country which need these transfers the most.
I go back to my original point, which is the withdrawal of a basic fundamental service. This goes back to Rowell-Sirois. Canadians have come to accept this commitment as a fundamental part of our citizenship, of sharing, of enabling all parts of the country to have an equitable, comparable and equal level of public services for our citizens, without having to bear an undue burden of taxes. The key participant in this program is a federal government, which is committed to ensuring that fiscal equity is maintained and is not allowed to erode as this government has allowed this program to erode and as we have seen with Bill C-69 and so many other measures
that have been introduced by this government since it has taken office.
I hope that members opposite will realize what is going on here, that they will see these measures in their broader perspective and, with the wisdom of the summer, will choose not to pass this legislation and will allow these transfer programs to be maintained so that the less well-off regions of the country can reach an equitable level of services and continue to provide for their citizens.

Mr. Speaker, I am not delighted to take part in this debate because I feel somewhat ashamed about my province and about this legislation. I want to start by pointing out that my province, with the same ideological drive as this government, is a province that deducts from welfare payments under the Canada Assistance Plan, federal benefits such as family allowances. It is the only province to do so and it makes deductions for orphans and survivor benefits. Now, that has to tell you something.
I do not blame the Government of Saskatchewan entirely for this. Because of the monetary and fiscal policies of this government, it has left provinces with little choice other than to make cutbacks. The problem is that provincial governments have made cutbacks in the wrong places. Imagine, Mr. Speaker, deducting family allowances from welfare payments and deducting payments for orphans and survivor benefits. It is un-Christian and uncivilized and immoral, if I have used enough adjectives.
The Tory government of Saskatchewan has set up a system where it decides who are the deserving and the undeserving poor. This sounds like the lords, the dukes, the kings, the queens and the princes of the Middle Ages. The government decides who are the deserving and the undeserving poor. If there is a breadwinner who will not take a job, why would you cut off the spouse and the children? Funds in Saskatchewan are being diverted from the Canada Assistance Plan to fund what is called Workfare programs. That sounds like Bill Vander Zalm of eight or 10 years ago, buy them a shovel. I do not recite this with any kind of pride, I feel some shame, because we were the province which led the way in
June 11, 1990

dealing with our poor, our unfortunate, our disabled and our sick and set an example for the entire country.
I want to say a word about the whole matter of keeping your word. Governments are no different than individuals. A person is only as good as his word. Whether you give it verbally with a handshake or whether you give it in writing, you do not change your word, unless you have negotiated a change with the person or other government to which you gave your word. If your word is no good, as far as I am concerned, you are no good as an individual. If the government's word is no good, this government is no good because previous governments, both Conservative and Liberal, gave their word under the Canada Assistance Plan, and under the funding for education and hospitalization and medicare, it gave its word.
I hope the province of British Columbia, supported by two other provinces, wins its case in the courts. I have a fond wish that this federal government would support those provinces, but then that would defeat its own case. The programs that this bill affects are the national programs, shared by federal and provincial governments, in which the federal government sets standards to apply everywhere, in rich and poor provinces as well as the middle ones. The provinces make the decisions as to what they are going to do under those programs which have been arrived at by agreement and under which governments at all levels gave their word.
Initially, in the late fifties, sixties and the early seventies under the various programs that had come in, the federal government was committed to pay half the cost as long as the provincial jurisdiction met the standards that were laid down in the national program to provide a degree of equity, fairness and co-operative federalism no matter where one lived in this country. At least, that is the way it was supposed to be, and that is the way it used to be. This bill destroys the way it is supposed to be now and the way it used to be.
When I listen to people talking about secondary education-an hon. member today made an excellent remark about what federal and provincial governments put into secondary education-it is not an expenditure. It is an investment. If one bought a blue chip stock on the stock market, it would be an investment. When the
Government Orders
students graduate, they go on to the labour market teaching in universities or whatever. They earn good incomes. If one wants to look at it strictly as a private enterpriser, the amount of taxes the government collects from them more than recovers whatever the costs were of federal and provincial contributions to their university education. In fact, not only the governments, but the country as a whole is ahead of the game.
Also, I want to say something about poverty and food banks. I am a child of the dirty thirties, if you think I might be a little childish now. I grew up in those years. I remember. What kind of a commentary is it on our country? There are more people lining up now for food banks than there were for soup kitchens in the dirty thirties. Elundreds of thousands line up every month for food banks. It amounts to one million or two million a year in a country that is wealthy. The federal funds will not keep up with what it costs. God knows most of that is handled by volunteers.
Volunteerism has always been there. However, there are costs that even the volunteers cannot handle. Imagine. We have more people lined up now in food banks- that is a nice name for what were called soup kitchens-than in the dirty thirties. Under child care, it is a choice, but what kind of a choice is this? Less spaces? Or less income assistance? Or, a combination of both? In the name of God, why would any self-respecting government with any kind of conscience resort to that? I do not understand.
When one talks about welfare payments and the government of the so-called "Devine" in Saskatchewan who would pick on orphans, widows and those who get family allowance while eligible for welfare, it has to be some kind of a sad commentary on the state of mind of a number of governments in this country. I include my own province and this Parliament.
I want to say something about universality. After 1949, not long after Louis St. Laurent became Prime Minister of Canada, old age pensions were made universal and were increased very modestly. It was no big deal in terms of the amount of money. But I will never forget when Prime Minister Louis St. Laurent publicly accepted his first old age pension cheque when he reached 65, not because he was bragging about it but to shore up the

June 11, 1990

whole principle of universality. I am sure he did not need the money; that was the last thing that was on his mind.
I was an avid reader of Hansard in those days. I subscribed to it. M. J. Coldwell and Stanley Knowles got up and complimented him for shoring up the principle of universality. It is a matter of right of every citizen of this country.
I just drew my first old age pension cheque. It arrived last Friday. I know I do not look a day over 29.
Hear, hear!

It arrived two weeks late, and I must have some words with the minister about that.
I take that as a matter of pride. From about 1950 or 1951, during my working years on the railroad and as party secretary in Saskatchewan, every year when I made up my income tax there was a line in there that said: "Old Age Security Fund". You paid 3 per cent or 4 per cent of your taxable income for the old age security fund. For 20-some years I paid for my old age pension, as did hundreds of thousands of Canadians. It was an extra tax.
Now when I meet the Minister of Finance in the washroom on the fifth floor, I ask him why. The only place I can meet him is in the washroom. I am not lying in wait for him. I ask him why. I paid for the damned thing. Now why do you have to claw it back? He says I am making too much money. I say fine, if you want to hit me one or two points on my income tax, which is the most fair system of all, fair ball, but don't touch the old age pension cheque, don't touch the family allowances. Those are universal, those are a matter of right which has been built into our system for the last 30 or 40 years for every Canadian citizen.
My Conservative colleagues spend a lot of time trying to get rich. The Premier of Saskatchewan hit orphans, widows and family allowance recipients. He found $300 million and some for the Cargill grain company for a fertilizer plant. I call that nothing but male bovine excrement, and you can translate that any way you like in Hansard.
I say to my colleagues on the government side that there are no pockets in the shroud and there are no cubbyholes in the coffin. All of us who can afford to pay more should be made to pay some more, and I include myself. But those of us who are in a position of fortune,
however limited it is, must pay more of a share. That means increasing income tax for high-income earners and corporations because, while we have been spending all the past months and years building a constitution, we must not build it at the expense of the poor, the deprived and those in deplorable situations through no fault of their own.
The test of how civilized and how Christian a society is, is how it treats its young, its sick and its old. This legislation flies in the face of those kinds of teachings. As Jesus said: "Inasmuch as you have done this unto the least of these you have done this unto me".
I urge government members to think about that, especially when they are having a prayer breakfast, and to apply it to this legislation and defeat it.

What difference does it make if the income tax is increased or the old age pension is taxed back? If the dollars were the same, what difference would it make? I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that this is pure semantics.
I appreciate the hon. member being able to quote scripture. That is honourable and enviable and we hope he will continue to do so.

Mr. Speaker, the difference is that when you have a universal program it is universal. You cannot be, if you will pardon the expression, half pregnant. It is either universal or it is not. If it is universal, you do not touch it with any other tax law.
That is the one side. Now let us separate it. The government needs more revenue. All the government has to do is go through its own books to see who is not paying their fair share. Damn it all, a teller working in a bank branch in Regina pays more income tax than the

bank she is working for. Don't talk to me about clawing back pensions.
I will only have three things when I am through in this place, although I am tempted to outlive my hon. friends around here. I will have my MP's pension, my Canada pension, and old age pension. That is it. I try to live up to there being no pockets in the shroud. As long as I have enough to be comfortable, to have a roof over my head, to keep my bills paid, to buiy myself and go on a holiday or two a year, what the hell more do you need? That is not living like a monk in the hills.
Surely, it is time for my hon. friend and all of us to fight this appeal to the worst in all of us, greed and selfishness. When is that going to happen? In responding to that point I want to say something that he had already implied, that he must have lied on the application because certainly that young fellow who just spoke is not 65 years of age.

I firmly believe that the proposed cuts in Established Programs Financing will have a disastrous effect on universities, colleges, hospital funding and the operation of hospitals.
"Let us not make hospitals, universities and colleges a battleground between the federal government and the provincial governments. Let us solve those problems, not on the backs of the hospitals and universities, let us solve those problems outside that arena".
Those who know the manner of my participation in the debates in this House will know that I rarely read directly from a script. I did so in the past few moments for a very particular reason. I will tell you what that reason is in a moment. Let me remind you what I have just said. I have said that I firmly believe that the cuts in the EPF funding would have disastrous effects on universities, hospitals, education generally, and so on.
I read that word for word because that conviction is mine. I am concerned that the cuts in EPF funding will do damage to the operation of hospitals, to the functioning of universities and colleges, and to the access of young Canadians in whatever province to an education beyond the secondary level. That is a conviction that I hold very strongly, and that is why I stand at this stage of the bill to protest one more time what the government is proposing to do.
I have read those words. Not only are they my conviction. They were, to be more accurate, also the conviction of the present Minister of Finance. A moment ago I read word for word what the gentleman who now occupies the post of the Minister of Finance said in this very House on March 24, 1982. Eight years ago and a bit the Minister of Finance in this government was saying exactly what I am saying here today: do not cut EPF, it will have a disastrous affect on universities, it will adversely affect hospital care. That is what the gentleman was saying eight years ago when he was sitting over here in opposition.
The first question is: Why did he change his tune? Why did he, the advocate as I am today and as I have been over the years of properly funded hospital care, of full participation by the federal government in the

funding of that hospital care, of adequately funded post-secondary education, and of adequate financial participation of the federal government in that post-secondary funding, change his tune on that particular issue? If we had the time we could show other inconsistencies between what the Minister of Finance said when he was in opposition and what he is perpetrating on the people of Canada at this particular time.
This bill brought in, in the guise of restraining the expenditure of government money, will indeed, as we have already said, play havoc with the lives of many people who because of the cutbacks in funding will not have as complete access to hospital care as they would have had without this cutback. It will play havoc with the lives of many young Canadians who because of these cutbacks will not have the same access to university education, community college education, or post-secondary education opportunities generally.
Let us for a moment look at the impact of some of the figures in various areas of this country. Do you realize, Mr. Speaker, that as a result of the actions of this Minister of Finance, this Prime Minister, and this government since they took office in 1984, the cumulative effects of the cutbacks in Established Programs Financing, and the reductions in federal transfer payments to the provinces in respect of this program amount to $684 million in the case of Newfoundland alone. That is from the time they started the cutbacks in 1986 until they run their course in 1995: $684 million. That is an awful lot of money for a small province such as Newfoundland and Labrador with a pretty limited capacity to pay and collect provincial tax revenues. At the same time it is an overwhelming burden in terms of the need to provide adequate university education and the need to provide adequate hospital care. That is $684 million less that the Newfoundland government will have received as a result of those particular cutbacks.
P.E.I, a smaller province than Newfoundland in terms of population, nevertheless will suffer a $155 million cutback over the life of the cutbacks in this bill and the bills preceding it since this government took office.
Nova Scotia will lose more than $1 billion that otherwise would have been transferred from the federal government to the provincial government in Nova Scotia so that that government could continue to meet its obligations in terms of post-secondary education and health care generally.
Often we hear the Prime Minister talk about how we are a caring society. Those are great words. It is difficult to see how that is supported by his actions as a leader of a government which is racking up new records in terms of its capacity to batter the weak, the less fortunate, and the old.
I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that after six years this government is not working. I am not saying that the government is not doing things. I am not saying that it is not busy. I am not saying that it is not trying things, but it is not functioning any more. If you back off for a moment and ask what a government ought to do, you will see that it is not doing what a government ought to be doing. It has stopped functioning as an effective government.
You can be effective without being completely popular. That is a different issue altogether, but this government is not carrying out its mandate. It is not functioning as the government of this country. This government no longer works, for a number of reasons.
First, it has lost the collective goodwill of the people. People out there do not trust this government any more. They do not believe in or give the government the benefit of the doubt any more. Normally in polls asking what kind of job the Prime Minister is doing or what kind of job the government is doing on a given day, you will find a fairly large pool of people who are prepared to give the government the benefit of the doubt. They are prepared to say that the government or the Prime Minister is doing a reasonable job, and so on and so forth.
Now, almost for the first time I believe in Canadian history, we are finding, and to a degree not experienced in other countries like Britain, Japan, West Germany, or the United States in similar polls, an overwhelming rejection of the Prime Minister and of the government of the day. The polls are absolutely astounding. From my standpoint in opposition it is encouraging, but in over-all terms these are absolutely astounding results, watershed
June 11, 1990

results, Rubicon results, in terms of what the country is saying about the performance of this Prime Minister and the performance of this government.
This government has lost the goodwill of the people of Canada. This government has certainly lost the goodwill of the people of Newfoundland and Labrador, the province that I have the honour to represent in this Chamber.
This government has also stopped listening to the people and the people sense it. What more graphic example could you have of that than what is happening in terms of the proposed goods and services tax. The government has been told by 85 per cent of the Canadian people, through a succession of polls, that the people of Canada do not like, do not want, do not believe in, or do not think they need the goods and services tax. Yet the government insists on ramming it down the throats of Canadians. This government is not listening to Canadians any more.
Third, it must be clearly evident to most Canadians now that this government is riding roughshod over the people of Canada. Many examples could be drawn of how this government and how the Prime Minister, in particular, ride roughshod over people's wishes, and how the Prime Minister takes the view that he is right all the time, whether it is on the cutbacks in Established Programs Financing, on the goods and services tax, on the closure of rural post offices, or on the abandonment of railway lines.
One of the more recent and more despicable examples occurred on national television in the last few days. I refer to the incident during the course of the Meech Lake coverage on Saturday morning, the case, as the press were calling it, of the missing clause. I watched the Prime Minister explain for about 10 minutes in the most complete detail. This was the case of the clause that was absent from the draft agreement Saturday morning, the clause that Mr. Wells, the Premier of Newfoundland and Labrador, wanted to have included in the document. That it was omitted was a matter of some concern for Mr. Wells.
The Prime Minister showed up and, in the scrum outside the Conference Centre, assured everybody that it was an innocent mistake and that if the press would stop asking him questions he would rush off inside the

door and fix it all. He said that it was just a typographical error, that some typist had slipped up and forgotten to include the paragraph that Mr. Wells wanted.
We all know, as subsequent events have shown us, that that is not what happened at all. We all know that it was a very deliberate act to leave that out. We all have it on the authority of a number of people that an instruction was given that that paragraph not be put in there. Mr. Wells is a premier representing a province of this country equal, I was led to believe, with every other province in this country. One would wonder in terms of the treatment we have gotten the last few days, but that is another issue.
Not only was an instruction given to delete the paragraph, but the Prime Minister stood there publicly, after having given that instruction, and said that it was not so. He assured us all that it was a completely innocent oversight that he was going fix as soon as he got inside the door.
We saw that kind of lie, that kind of untruth being played out on national television by the master of sleight of hand. I am not saying the Prime Minister had to accommodate every concern. I have some feelings on that, and they are not different from those of Mr. Wells.
However, to stick with the example, whether or not all the concerns should have been accommodated, the very least you would expect from the Prime Minister is some candour on the issue, either to say nothing or to tell it as it is instead of standing there for 10 minutes reading into the record what in terms of subsequent events was shown to be a clear falsehood, an absolute untruth, with no basis in truth at all. His assertion that it was an innocent typographical error, that somebody erred in the typing pool and left out the paragraph and he was going to fix it as soon as he got in the door, was wrong. He knew at the time he said it that it was wrong, blatantly wrong.
When Canadians have come to expect that kind of duplicity, that kind of double-talk from the Prime Minister of this country, is it any wonder that I can read into the record what the Minister of Finance said a few years ago and then demonstrate to you by holding up Bill C-69 that now the Minister of Finance, with the acquiescence of the Prime Minister, is doing the exact opposite?
