Mr. Speaker, the hon. member mentioned his own province and how this bill affects it. He discussed medicare and post-secondary education at some length. However, what does he see down the road as the real effects of these cuts? It is all right for the government members to get up and say that they have got to cut the deficit. We all know that. However, they are really doing it on the backs of the other governments in this country, and we have to include municipal governments because the buck will eventually stop there too.
What effect does the hon. member really see these cuts having on provincial government administrations? How does he see them affecting the division of the tax dollars between federal and provincial governments in Canada?
Another member talked about the Rowell-Sirois report, one of the most thorough studies of financial divisions and jurisdiction ever held in this country. How does he envision the available tax dollars being divided in the future if the federal government is going to continue to slough off what is their burden onto the shoulders of the provinces, the municipalities and John Q. Public in this country?

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my colleague and friend for Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke for the question. I say to him, do not fall for that line about cutting the deficit, and I know he does not fall for it. I know he put it to me as a preamble to his question. But I say to the Canadian people and to myself, let us not fall for this absolute nonsense about cutting the deficit.
If cutting the deficit was such a priority, then let me use another cliche. I always believed and was taught that charity begins at home. If there is to be some effort in cutting the deficit, why is it that we see the government, the Prime Minister, and the ministers still living very high on the hog. This burning desire to cut the deficit does not seem to stop the Prime Minister when it comes time to fly the limousines down to Costa Rica or to generally live high on the hog here in Canada.
We can take examples that in dollar terms do not mean a lot to this government in terms of total budget, but they mean a lot to the people who are living out there on welfare and whose welfare is going to be further threatened by this particular bill.
So, I cannot get very excited, Mr. Speaker, about cutting the deficit when I watch the way this government operates.
Let me come to the second part of the question of my friend, the hon. member for Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke. He asked, what do I see down the road as the effects. I say to him that we are seeing the effects. Already, I am talking to young people who cannot go to university. Already, I am talking to provincial finance ministers. I talked to the one from my own province in the last few hours who tells me that it is becoming very difficult to make ends meet, to meet the financial needs of the university and the hospitals in Newfoundland and Labrador because of the effects of this bill. The cumulative effect of this bill and the others before it since this government came to office is $684 million. That is $684 million less that Newfoundland is going to get to pay its
June 11, 1990

medical bills, its university bills than it would have received if this bill was not before us.
Provincial governments are going to have to either cut back services or raise their taxes. A larger segment of the total revenue is going to have to come from provincial tax dollars. There again, if there were time and I were to digress away from this issue, I could draw a parallel between what was happening last week in the constitutional talks and the way they were being manipulated and what is happening here. It is the same whole mug's game where you shift the blame all the time to somebody else.
In the case of this particular bill cutting back expenses, funding for university and health costs expenditures, the government is shifting the blame to the provincial treasurers, the provincial finance ministers, the provincial premiers so they will be blamed if they raise provincial taxes, if they cut back on health care and on university education programs.
I say to my friend from Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke, that is the sadness of it all. The people most affected, the elderly, university students, the people on social assistance, are having to put up with this continuing smoke and mirrors game by this government that smiles while putting the knife in all the time.

Mr. Speaker, this bill is so wide ranging that one can talk about almost anything. I would like to first outline the specifics of the bill. What Bill C-69 actually does is freeze federal transfer payments for the next two years to the provinces under the Established Programs Financing, which is another term for transfer payments with regard to post-secondary education and health care. It limits the increase for federal transfer payments to Ontario, to British Columbia and Alberta under the Canada Assistance Plan.
It is eliminating the Canadian Exploration Incentives Program which is hurting small exploration companies. It freezes public utilities income tax transfers over the next two years.
Government Orders
The budget cutbacks alone to these four programs amount to $1 billion in 1990-91, $1.8 billion in 1991-92, and a total of $8.4 billion over the next five fiscal years that the provinces are not going to get. The cutbacks to transfer payments to all provinces for these essential areas of post-secondary education and health care, and cutbacks to transfer payments to Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia under the Canada Assistance Plan, will force the provinces to simply increase taxes.
This government is not cutting the deficit, as my hon. friend just said a while ago. It is transferring the debt to the provinces, or passing the buck, as it is called. As a result of this bill passing, and the cutting of transfer payments to the provinces by this government, the provinces are going to have to collect another $576 per taxpayer in their provinces over the next five years. When Canadians see their provincial taxes go up, they are actually paying the taxes for this Minister of Finance who is passing the buck to the provinces.
This is not the first time it has happened. It is the third time that the Conservative government has attacked the Established Programs Financing or transfer payments since 1986. Cumulatively, these transfer cutbacks between 1986 and 1987 right up to 1994 and 1995 will amount to the astronomical sum of $31.1 billion, of which $22.2 billion should have been allocated to health care and $8.9 billion to post-secondary education.
I just want to repeat in particular, the figure of $22.2 billion that should be allocated to health care and is not going to be by this federal government. Is it any wonder that the people out there are worried about the medicare program across Canada because the federal government is backing away from its share of the contribution and indeed its responsibility. Then they say the people who talk about it are fear-mongering. What a farce.
An interesting conversation took place today between me and the Minister of Finance across the floor. I like to keep reminding the Minister of Finance that in a speech in Toronto in August, 1984 he said that he would certainly not attack the deficit by increasing taxes but would rather do it by cutting government programs.

June 11, 1990
Government Orders
Not only has he increased taxes 31 times, and the GST will be the thirty-second time, he has certainly kept his promise about cutting programs. Right here, we see where he is cutting these transfer payments to the provinces by over $31 billion in a five-year period. They are not just programs, they are institutions of this country, namely, medicare and post-secondary education.
He has cut the other government programs with a vengeance. The national debt is still growing. The sad part is that he is not making any gains because the national debt of the country has more than doubled since the government took office. The simplicity of the economic measures promised by the Minister of Finance in 1984 can simply be classified as schoolboy rhetoric.
If the provinces decide not to increase taxes, they will be forced to make cutbacks. In turn, hospitals will have to close beds, limit costly operations or find other reductions. Students will have to face higher tuition fees, overcrowded classes or other cost-cutting measures.
On March 24, 1982, the Minister of Finance had the following to say in the House, and I do not think this quote can be repeated often enough:
Let us not make hospitals, universities and colleges a battleground
between the federal government and the provincial governments.
Let us solve those problems, not on the backs of hospitals and
universities; let us solve those problems outside of that arena.
Here he has brought his very solution to it and he has brought those things right back into the arena. In Bill C-69 that is before the House today, he is doing the very things he suggested should not be done when he was sitting in the opposition in the House of Commons.
Today, he said that I was living in the past. When the Minister of Finance makes a promise or a commitment, if one reminds him of it, one is living in the past. I brought him a little more up to date and mentioned his recent statement with regard to post-secondary education and medicare. It seems that when the Minister of Finance makes commitments and one reminds him of them, one is talking about the past. I wonder what he would say if we criticized him for something we thought he was going to say in a year from now. I do not think
that would be very good logic to follow. The Minister of Finance always has a way to slough these things off.
The reason for the Minister of Finance said that I was living in the past must be due to the fact that the minister has been making commitments for so long, that to him these commitments have become traditional, rather than becoming something new. As soon as he says them, they are old hat.
The real fact that we see in this bill today is the fact that the provinces are being dumped on by the federal government of Canada. The Minister of State for Privatization, when he was once before a legislative committee I was a member of, complained because the provinces had little or no debt and they should have. He was ready to dump on them then, and he certainly has since.
It is very important at this stage to come out simply with the real challenge about this. It was mentioned in the House today that the Province of Ontario had a balanced budget this year. Because the provinces have no debt, in the eyes of the federal government, that seems to be a sin. Because they have a balanced budget, it wants to dump more on to them.
When these transfer cuts were announced, a few days after the budget was tabled British Columbia and Ontario announced that they would challenge the cuts to the Canada Assistance Program in court. This legal battle could delay implementation of this measure until the court makes its decision. Alberta supports the action taken by these two provinces.
The contesting provinces believe that the Canada Assistance Plan can only be modified after a year's notice and with provincial consent. After all, the province must be given some notice if it is going to get its financial house in order, instead of having this cut thrust on it overnight.
Also, the government did not seek consent of the provinces, so neither one of these conditions have been met. Right now the provinces look as if they are in a very good position.
With respect to post-secondary education, the Prime Minister betrayed, once again, his own promise to have first-class education for our youth and, in so doing, made a mockery of the national task force on education that he had created. On August 25, 1989, the Prime Minister stated: "This government will carry its fair share of the
June 11, 1990

burden to ensure that all young Canadians receive a first-class education as they confront a world-class challenge".
One cannot challenge someone to do something one minute and pull the rug out from underneath them then next.
When the provinces are called upon to make up the difference in financing important items such as post-secondary education and medicare, the money must come from somewhere else. There is a very important part to that with respect to the Canada Assistance Plan. Cuts in assistance to the poorest in Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia contradict the government's commitment to "come to the aid of those who are in need".
The poor in these three provinces are just as poor as those in any other of the provinces. Moreover, British Columbia and Ontario, supported by Alberta, are carrying on their court case challenging that budgetary item right now as we study this bill.
These are great words by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance, but there is no commitment. The additional financial pressure that will be brought to bear on provincial governments will affect other services provided by provincial governments such as the building of roads and forestry. Agriculture and forestry are industries that need a lot of help today, and energy projects are very expensive, as we know.
We have a major issue here in eastern Ontario with regard to Elighway 17, travelling up the Ottawa Valley from Ottawa. There have been a lot of unfortunate deaths on that highway, but they have not all been attributable, by any means, to the highway itself.
I would like to make a very important point. The amount of money that Ontario lost when the federal government cut its transfer payments this year would have practically built that entire highway. The province has announced the building of Highway 316 from the 401 into Ottawa, four lanes. After 123 years of Confederation, it will be the first four-lane highway into the National Capital from southern Ontario. It has announced the continuation of building of a four-lane highway from the end of the Queensway to Arnprior. The highway continues from there is for another 75 miles or so. That will come, but I want to point out that financial stress has been placed on the province of
Government Orders
Ontario by the lack of transfer payments from the federal government and indeed through Bill C-69 today.
It is very important to note that the province of Ontario, which faces drastic cuts in transfer payments, is now faced with major construction items in eastern Ontario to be done over a very short time-frame. There were 42 years of Conservative government at Queen's Park in Ontario and eastern Ontario was neglected. Today, the province of Ontario under Premier Peterson is faced with catch-up programs because of neglect during those more than four decades of Conservative government in Ontario.
There were times when 14 out of 15 members of the Ontario legislature from eastern Ontario were Conservative members. So there is no penalty for not voting the right way. They voted for the government and still did not get those improvements and eastern Ontario was neglected.
When the Hon. Joe Greene was Minister of Agriculture and later Minister of Energy, he called Highway 17 the Ottawa Valley's goat trail in a speech in the House of Commons more than 25 years ago. If he were here today, he would be very interested in the debate that is going on on that issue now.
I am simply saying that it is unfair to call upon the present provincial government under Premier Peterson to do in a half dozen years what the previous Conservative government failed to do in 42 years.
As a finale, I mention that I asked a question previously about the Rowell-Sirois report and the division of finances between the provinces and the federal government. I am absolutely convinced that, with the way we are going, we will need another in-depth study of the financial structure of the country.
The changes in transfer payments are undermining the basic financial arrangements of the country that have been in place for years. They have served the country well at both federal and provincial levels and now that they are changing, there will be some bad effects and things will certainly be mismanaged as a result of that.
No one wants to see another great depression such as the one in the thirties that brought about that report. It affected families. People could not even pay their taxes. It was a lost generation. Everybody has a right to fair education and to medicare in the country.

June 11, 1990
Government Orders
I can only say in conclusion that the government is going to have to change its mind. It is going to have to start living up to the basic agreements under the Rowell-Sirois Commission report and get back on track and pay proper transfer payments to the provinces if we are going to maintain any standard of living in that regard.

Mr. Speaker, my original intention was not to enter into this debate, but when I realized that Bill C-69 is the largest cut to social programs in Canadian history-the largest cut that slashes health, education, welfare, child care and transition shelter spending-I would be negligent in my duty as a member of Parliament not to lend my voice in protest at the actions of the government.
Is it not ironic today that during Question Period we heard the government defend major increases to its top bureaucrats, increases of $40,000, $50,000, $60,000, and I heard in one case of over $100,000. The justification here is that we have got to make these top management positions competitive with the private sector.
Indeed, in the last number of years we have seen tremendous increases in the salaries and the dividends that the top of the corporate sector has received. On the same day that the government can justify these tremendous increases on the upper income scale, it is introducing Bill C-69 that would cap the transfer of the assistance payments from the federal government to three provincial governments, the governments of Ontario, Alberta, and British Columbia. Perhaps those are the provinces where the poor need assistance the most, because the cost of living and the cost of housing, particularly in cities like Toronto and Vancouver, have made it almost impossible for poor people to continue to live in those urban centres.
On the same day that the government attempts to justify these tremendous increases to its top echelons in the Crown corporations and departments, it attempts to move through a bill that cuts back on programs like medicare and post-secondary education. As a country we are in a period of tremendous economic transition, much of it brought about by things like the free trade agreement. This brings about tremendous human dislocation. People who have worked in their jobs, developed a career, developed skills, all at once find that those skills are no longer needed. It is a time when those people need some support, for education, for retraining and as a
social net. This government has been attacking that social net. On the one hand, it has created a greater need for a social net, and on the other hand, it is yanking that social net away. I do not believe the people of Canada will endorse and support this.
Of course, we hear the government justify this because it says it is fighting the deficit. I have no problems with that. Let us not forget that it is not the poor of this country who are to be blamed for the deficit. They did not create the deficit, and the victims should not be attacked. We have heard Tories say that we are living beyond our means and that we should tighten our belts.
Looking at Canada's record, compared to the other industrialized countries, such as OECD countries, what we spend on social programs as a percentage of Gross Domestic Product is the second lowest. We spend less on social programs, on health, education, welfare, family allowance, medicare, you name it, as a percentage of our Gross Domestic Product than Holland, Italy, Germany, Denmark, Sweden, Great Britain or Ireland. Only the United States, as a percentage of its Gross Domestic Product, spends less on social programs than we do.
Do not tell me it is the poor and the social programs of this country which have created the deficit. Do not blame the victims. This is the traditional Tory line of blaming the victims, and saying that the people on welfare have got it too good, that our medicare program is too rich, that our child care program is just too expensive and too costly. If the people in Germany, Holland, Italy, Sweden, and Denmark are able to afford programs that ensure that there is decent medicare, that there is child care, that the elderly are taken care of in dignity, that there is a proper education system, particularly in terms of retraining and higher education, then in heaven's name, I cannot understand why a country as rich as Canada, with our tremendous resources, with our sparse population is not able to afford the same.
I want to touch particularly on the cutbacks to the EPF program and the effect that this will have on higher education. Earlier this spring, I visited several universities around the country. When I visited Carleton University, here in Ottawa, I was told by students that at times there is a five or six day waiting period for a particular book at the library and even then, when they get there they might only be able to have this resource book for maybe an hour or two, because the university cannot
June 11, 1990

afford to replenish its library with the needed research material. I visited the university at the Lakehead, where I was told that the plant and equipment in their research facilities had been bought at the beginning of this decade and now need to be improved. Repairs are needed and equipment needs to be updated and they cannot afford it. Mr. Speaker, I visited the university at Lethbridge and the university in Calgary and I heard about the same problems, that the tuition fees are being increased, the size of classroom is being expanded and the ratio between the instructor and the number of students is increasing. The same problem exists at the university in my home city of Regina, a university that I attended. I was president of the students' council in the 1960s. At that time we talked about a community of scholars.
I walk in those university halls today and it is not a community of scholars. It is a McDonald's fast food chain. That is what higher education has come to in this country, a fast food outlet with huge lecture halls and professors with whom you will never have an opportunity to have an intellectual discussion or discourse. Forget about the notion of the community of scholars.
Our universities are becoming second rate. They do not have the research equipment in order to help graduate first-rate researchers. That is what this country needs. This is what we need if we are going to grow into the 21st century.
We need scientists. Our young people need a world first-class education. Unfortunately we are becoming a second-rate nation because our education system is becoming second rate.
That is the saddest part of all. We are denying and robbing our young people of the possibility of being able to get good jobs because they are not getting a first-class education. I find that so sad, Mr. Speaker.
What this government is doing with Bill C-69 is attacking the poor through such measures as medicare and post-secondary education, measures that help the
Government Orders
young, the old, the aged and the sick. Now they must bear the burden of fighting the deficit.
Meanwhile the Governor of the Bank of Canada and his staff and minions are able to get large increases in their pay. The upper echelon of the Public Service is getting good, fat bonuses.
It is gross.

Mr. Speaker, my colleague says it is gross. It is gross that on the one hand we have the attack by the Tory government on the poor, and on the other hand it is helping the well-to-do. What a mix of priorities.
I think we all feel ashamed to be Canadians when we begin to develop a record like this. It is denying our future; it is denying those who are less fortunate than ourselves in our society; it is resulting in a less caring society and so therefore a less civilized society, all in a country so rich with resources and wealth.
Those are the comments I wish to make in this debate. I join with my colleagues in protesting and speaking against an act which is the largest cutback in social programs in the history of this country.

Mr. Speaker, I want to take a couple of minutes to commend my colleague from Regina for a very eloquent speech, commenting on Bill C-69.
This legislation in a very fundamental way will change the social contract of this country. These are changes that this Conservative government has embarked upon some time ago.
We remember all too well the promises the Prime Minister made that social programs were to be a sacred trust. We also remember that this same government, this same Prime Minister who promised that social programs would be a sacred trust, has cut back on benefits to the elderly, cut back on family allowances, and has cut back on unemployment insurance benefits.
As well, we know that the provisions of this government's so-called restraint-obviously there is no restraint for senior civil servants in this government-has frozen contributions for legal aid, has cut in real terms programs for young offenders, and we know they have cut funding for social housing in this country as well.

June 11, 1990
Government Orders
The effect of Bill C-69 is particularly serious in my province of British Columbia. As we know, it has imposed a cap on transfers under the Canada Assistance Plan of 5 per cent per year in the provinces of Ontario, Alberta, and my own province of British Columbia.
The combined effects of Bill C-96, the budget, and Bill C-33 will mean for British Columbia that up until 1995 we will have lost, in real terms, over $3 billion which would otherwise be directed to the province of British Columbia. That will be in the area of health care, in post-secondary education, and in a number of other important areas. All these areas under the Vander Zalm Social Credit Government are already reeling because of devastating cutbacks.
With regard to health care, we have seen people who are on waiting lists for heart surgery actually dying because of the heartlessness of the Vander Zalm Social Credit Government, now aided and abetted by the Conservatives.
We have seen devastating cuts in post-secondary education in my own constituency in Simon Fraser University and the B.C. Institute of Technology. Both of them are suffering from crowding, cutbacks in resources for libraries and research, and all the other areas that my colleague from Regina has pointed out so eloquently. We know as well that in terms of the health care effects of Bill C-69 this has dealt a very serious blow to the Canada Health Act. The executive director of the nurses' association has said that the Minister of Finance has just sounded a death knell to the Canada Health Act. As my colleague has indicated, and I see the Speaker signalling that I should wrap up my comments, this bill will attack the people who are already the poorest in our country.
I want to ask my colleague if he would like to comment briefly with respect to the impact that this bill will have, particularly on the poor in the provinces of Ontario, British Columbia, and Alberta where after all almost half the recipients of the Canada Assistance Plan are located. Many aboriginal people are already struggling in devastating poverty, a condition that has been described as a national shame by the chief commissioner of the Canadian Human Rights Commission. I wonder if my very distinguished colleague could comment on this point.

Mr. Speaker, yes, indeed it gives me pleasure to respond to my colleague's question.
I suspect the best way of describing the results of these measures that the government has taken on the poor is to say that it is sentencing the poor to deeper poverty. It is affecting, in particular, poor people in metropolitan areas like Vancouver and Toronto and like Edmonton and Calgary as well where the price of housing increased significantly in the last number of years and where to pay the rent now has become a substantial part of people's incomes. Certainly the people in lower income groups have not seen their wages rise the way the cost of living has risen for them.
I remember one case of a person I know quite well who lives in the city of Vancouver. She is a single parent, works in a restaurant, and has some cooking abilities. She clears around $1,200 to $1,300 a month. She spends $450 of that on rent and $450 on day care. That amounts to $900, which leaves her about $400 to pay for her transportation, food, and all the other necessities in life. This is a hard working person who is trying to keep off the welfare roles and who wants to live an active and productive life. It is not easy for people in that situation. In fact it is darn hard. I wish the government would show some consideration and heart for these people, but it does not do so. Its fixation on the deficit is such that it is willing to inflict greater hardships on our poor people in order to solve the problem and the economic mess that it has created. I find that unconscionable.

Mr. Speaker, just a couple of words in the dying moments of this debate.
The bill before the House says in its title "restraint of government expenditures". The very areas that it restrains government expenditures in are in the areas of health and education. If there were two areas that one could come up with in which government should not restrain its spending, it would have to be in health and education. Those are the two main, basic areas. They are the two areas in which we need more expenditures, health and education.
Today, in the federal riding of Gander-Grand Falls we have to send people to Halifax, Nova Scotia, to receive certain types of medical treatment not available in the province of Newfoundland. I am referring to the fact that the only litho triptic machine in Atlantic
June 11, 1990

Canada is in a hospital in Halifax, Nova Scotia. That is the only one of which I know.
Four hundred and fifty Newfoundlanders a year get on a plane and go from one of our airports in their local community and travel all the way to Halifax, Nova Scotia, to wait in line for a relatively uncomplicated procedure that was invented about 10 years ago. There are machines that are perfected that cost around $2 million. When one talks about the cost of hospital machines one has to keep in mind that the major cost is in actually operating it sometimes.
There are 450 people a year who have to go to another province to receive treatment. The cost is very great to the provincial treasury, but it is greater to the people who have to make that journey. To modernize at a time when more expenditures are needed, when provincial governments are struggling to keep up-to-date with their machinery in hospitals, the federal government turns around and announces that it is cutting its money for the operation of hospitals. What used to be called the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Care Act was changed in 1977 and is now called block funding.
As well, a major problem with a student going to Memorial University in Newfoundland is this. Can the student take the course that he or she needs to take in order to go to a professional school? In other words, you go into someone's house and ask: "How is your son or daughter doing"? The mother looks up and says: "Well, not too bad, but they can't seem to be able to take the courses they need in order to get the degree or in order to go on to a professional school". Just imagine, in this day and age, a student registered in the university, paid the tuition and cannot do the courses they need to do because there are not enough places.
Shame.
Just imagine the major problems of a student going to university today .
It is shameful.

At a time when that is happening, what does the federal government do? It turns around and cuts transfer payments for post-secondary education to the provinces.
Government Orders
I suppose it would be bad enough if we could make up for it on the provincial end. If you cut $684 million in transfers from the budget of the province of Newfoundland from 1986 to 1995, if the federal government were doing something that would make up for the loss, then fine and dandy, we would end up square and would at least be able to progress.
Speaking of the riding of Gander-Grand Falls, we just had a paper mill close because the company is building a new one in Alabama. Another one is in Venezuela on the Oronoco River.
With faster growing trees.

Yes, faster growing trees, cheaper labour, encouragement of the federal Government of Canada to invest in the United States, invest in other parts of the world at a time when we face cuts in these areas, when industries are closing, on the encouragement of the Government of Canada, increasing their business in the United States, the Government of Canada turns around and actually issue up to 58 factoiy freezer trawler licences for foreign nations to fish off our coast.
Who speaks for Canada?

They are licensed inside the 200-mile zone. If you were to say that is $1 a pound for every pound of fish they caught, on last year's figures that would be $1 billion.
If we were to tell the Soviet Union, Cuba, Norway, and all the foreign nations and all of these people that we want to go over there and fish off their coasts, we would be blown out of the water.
The Government of Canada has just increased their licences. For the first time in our history we have mackerel being caught off the coast of Newfoundland and Nova Scotia and in the Cabot Strait. The government just gave out licences last week to the U.S.S.R. to fish off Labrador and northern Newfoundland to within 12 miles of the coast. The point is if you made it up on a dollar-per-pound basis, that would be $1 billion and Newfoundland could build hospitals and get its litho triptic machines. But, we do not see any of that. We see just the reverse happening.
All in all, this bill should really be defeated by the House of Commons. It should be thrown in the ashcan of history. It does not deserve to be before the House at

Adjournment Debate
this time or at any other time and we hope that government members will vote against it.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on this occasion to discuss a question I asked in the House of Commons on April 3. The question was directed to the Minister of Fisheries.
My concern was that in view of the extraordinary gap in the surveillance and control mechanism off Canada's coastline, the longest in the world, and particularly in light of Recommendation 22 of the Harris Report, which talked about additional resources to undertake the task of surveillance and control, particularly in fisheries surveillance, I asked the minister to inform the House what plans he had to redress this well known and serious deficiency.
Either the minister misunderstood my question or he chose to answer one particular portion of it because, in fact, he did discuss one aspect but it was the aspect of the recent contract that had been signed. That was with Provincial Airways in Newfoundland for the two King Air 200 Beechcraft aircraft that were going to carry out their surveillance in lieu of the trackers. I think the contracts were to the tune of $28 million. I was delighted to hear that but I had already known that. In fact, let me read what Recommendation 22 of the Harris Report says: "The Government of Canada should undertake the provision of additional patrol vessels" and I stress patrol vessels, "for offshore surveillance to provide adequate on-site action in respect of violations reported by aircraft or by observers".
My concern is essentially for the vessels, which is a follow-up to any surveillance that may be done. Surveillance alone is not good. The business is surveillance and control, if you are interested in controlling your fisheries areas.
Since the mid-seventies off the east coast of Newfoundland, there has been a tremendous change in the pace in the fisheries. There have been more people involved, there have been more foreigners, more species being fished, better technology and larger ships going out to a much greater distance than had taken place in the mid-seventies.
Before I go any further, I would make the statement that it would be very hard to deny that the surveillance and control activities that we have now are probably less than we had in 1975, with a tremendous magnitude increase in the fisheries that are taking place.
June 11, 1990

When we look at surveillance and control in Canada, there are really three aspects of this. Right now, the offshore patrols are a combination of air surveillance, ship patrols and observers that we place aboard most of the foreign vessels out to the 200-mile limit. Let's forget about the observers. I will not talk about them any more this evening. I would like to concentrate on air patrols in a general sense.
Canada has the world's largest coastline, 60,000 coastline miles. To patrol that, we have a total of 18 Aurora aircraft; we used to have 25 or 26 trackers but they will eventually be gone. To my knowledge, in the east coast, we have recently contracted for two Beechcraft King Air 200s, which granted us a very effective aircraft with the new Litton radar. I believe there is one more in the making. That is 18, 19, 20, or 21 aircraft, if you count them. The 18 Aurora are long-range maritime patrol. The coastline is 60,000 linear miles.
The Netherlands has a coastline of 228 miles. It uses roughly the same number, 13 maritime patrol aircraft.
Japan has 5,000 linear miles of coastline. It has presently 130 maritime patrol aircraft and is about to order another 100.
If you want to put this another way, Mr. Speaker, Japan with one-tenth the coastline has 10 times the patrol effort off its coast, and Holland has roughly the same number of maritime patrol aircraft to patrol one-two hundred and fiftieth of the coastline.
Mr. Speaker, I think you can see the comparisons there which indicate that either these two countries are awfully high or we are awfully low. I would suggest that it is the latter.
I want now to look at the specific recommendation related to the patrol vessels. As I stand here tonight there are only patrols vessels off Canada's east coast. The two vessels are the William Colley and the Cape Roger. I believe the Cape Roger is in refit now. Statistically there is really one and a half patrol vessels to patrol the east coast of Canada and the south coast of Newfoundland.
When you look at the area that is covered, Mr. Speaker, and just picture now the south coast of Newfoundland, all the area of the northern cod out around the Grand Banks and way up as far north as Baffin
Adjournment Debate
Island, there are just two vessels. To say that that is inadequate is a gross understatement. In fact to say it is a token is ludicrous. It is nothing more than a joke. It is a joke. The brunt of the joke is Newfoundlanders and Atlantic Canadians. Out of the two patrol vessels one is stationed on the Banks pretty well all the time, and the other one therefore has to patrol that vast area.
Mr. Speaker, as anybody with a maritime background would tell you, that is a joke. That is the best way I can put it.
The point of this whole business is that surveillance and control is a team effort. The aircraft locate and identify, but they are incapable of actually taking any action that would force the proper follow-on from these illegal pursuits.
Aircraft certainly has some advantages, that is, they cannot be rammed by an aggressive trawler, as the Saguenay was rammed by the Concordia just before Christmas last year. I have to stress that you can locate as many fishermen as you can, but unless there is a surface vessel to go out and actually board and examine the catch, and unless there is enough aircraft to continue with continuous patrol, then you are in serious trouble.
I would like to make a suggestion. We have 21 trawlers now that seem to be of surplus use, I guess largely because of the reduction in the effort of the fisheries which has been a forced effort due to the dismal state of our stocks. These 21 fisheries vessels include the six mid-distance fleet off Newfoundland that have been decommissioned.
I would like to suggest that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, the Minister of National Defence, and perhaps the Secretary of State for External Affairs get together to see if somehow we can acquire these vessels. We can lease them, rent them, or perhaps even buy them. We can man them with qualified skippers, maybe some of the skippers from these trawlers who are out of work. We might even consider putting them in the naval reserve and having them operate under the Maritime Coastal Defence Organization that was recently formed in Maritime Command.
Mr. Speaker, I can assure you that if this is not a no cost it is certainly a low cost recommendation that I believe-in fact I am seriously convinced-should have further investigation. I leave that to the goodwill and

Adjournment Debate
imagination of the Ministers of National Defence and Fisheries and Oceans.

speakeroldname: Mr. Michel Champagne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Forestry)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Forestry

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak on behalf of the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Valcourt) and remind the hon. member that recommendation 22 of the Harris Report suggests that the Government of Canada make arrangements to increase the number of ships assigned to maritime surveillance.
The purpose is to provide sufficient resources to be able to follow up on violations sighted by airplanes or pointed out by observers. This measure will also make it possible to combine the use of helicopters and smaller patrol boats for surveillance of coastal fisheries. Similar recommendations were made by the Scotia-Fundy task force on the ground fishery. In the course of departmental consultations throughout Atlantic Canada, the industry, fishermens' organizations and provincial governments also pointed out the need for more efficient and effective surveillance, both inside and outside the Canadian zone.
More efficient and effective surveillance and enforcement of the regulations will require full integration of all aspects of the surveillance program, including air surveillance, coverage by observers, surveillance at sea and ashore, and monitoring of quotas.
The Department of Fisheries and Oceans recently awarded a contract to Airways Limited for 3,815 hours of air surveillance of the deep sea fisheries in 1990-91. This represents more than twice the number of hours of surveillance provided by the trackers of the Department of National Defence in recent years. The new surveillance which will be in addition to 420 hours of flying by the Aurora aircraft provided free of charge by DND, represents a substantial upgrading of our deep sea fisheries air surveillance program off the Atlantic coast.
The minister realizes that effective management of fish stocks means that we must have appropriate and adequate air surveillance and control. To this end, the department will monitor and assess all components of its
surveillance and regulatory programs to determine the levels of air, sea and land patrols to be maintained to guarantee effective management of Canada's fish stocks.

Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George-Bulkley
Valley): Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today in the House to follow up on a question I put to the Minister of the Environment, which in his absence ended up being answered by the Minister of Forestry. This was on May 7, which was in National Forest Week. This was a very important week in Canada, something of which I think all Canadians are aware.
The question that I put to the minister at the time was along these lines. I asked him in light of the commitment and the talk from the government about the importance of our environment and the announcement of The Green Plan what kind of commitment there was from the government to plant some trees. It was a very simple question.
During National Forest Week and on Earth Day everybody across the country-indeed, across North America and the world-were out doing their thing for the environment. Part of that was people planting trees. Everybody was out planting trees except for this government.
The reason we call on this government to tiy and plant some trees I think is pretty obvious. We know all the concerns about global warming, the role our forests play in our ecosystems, and all the employment that people from coast to coast get from our forests. There are over 300 communities dependent on the forest industry.
How does the federal government plant trees? It does it through a very effective vehicle that many provinces have come to be aware of. It is through forestry agreements, as they are called, that are signed with all provinces. They have been used in different parts of Canada for different purposes, often for research, assisting with the development of new species, and what have you.
In British Columbia, my home province, and in my own riding there has been a great deal of assistance given to replanting harvested land. This is because the government of the day failed to do any serious work in reforestation or any intensive silvicultural work, which

left these lands unproductive with no seedlings to grow and no future for forests.
The government of the day came up with what are called the Forest Resource Development Agreements. I have raised this issue in the House on a number of occasions, primarily because we are faced now with the incredible situation that despite the rhetoric of the government and its so-called concern for the environment, it has allowed forestry agreements in Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Alberta to expire well over a year ago. In British Columbia our forest agreement expired on March 31. We have been without a forest agreement for some 72 days now, despite six commitments by the Minister of Forestry to the people of British Columbia. One of the main commitments was that he would find the money in the Supplementary Estimates or elsewhere. We asked the department to produce that information for the forestry committee two months ago, and it has yet to find out any of that basic information.
The minister also made a commitment to us that he would have an agreement signed well before the planting season would start. The planting season for seedlings across the country varies, but in some cases in British Columbia it started as early as April. The time is coming fast, if it has not passed already, for contractors to gear up to plant trees. A number of contractors in British Columbia are now scaling down operations in the light of the absolute failure of the federal Conservative government and the Socred government in British Columbia to reach and sign a forest agreement. It is critical that we do that in this country.
I want to read into the record from Forestry Canada's own 1990-1991 Estimates. This is important information for all of us. It concerns how many trees we are planting versus how much we are harvesting and what we have left over. I quote:
- in 1987, of a total harvest estimated at just under 1 million hectares, 285,000 hectares were successfully planted or seeded while a further 500,000 hectares are estimated to have regenerated naturally, leaving a shortfall of 210,000 hectares.
These figures are likely small c conservative. Just under 250,000 hectares are being added to the non-for-ested land in this country because of the lack of forest agreements, the lack of the kind of forest management policies that we should have in this country. We have called upon this government and the provincial govern-

Mr. Speaker, I was greatly interested in the comments of my colleague who, in the course of his remarks, stated that in recent years the federal government, our government, the Progressive Conservative Party has not accomplished anything at all in terms of reforestation. I would remind him that since 1984 our government increased the forestry budget by more than 300 per cent. Our government also signed in excess of $1.2 billion worth of investment agreements with the Canadian provinces, including British Columbia, Quebec, Newfoundland and all the other provinces. We are talking about investments of more than $1.3 billion dollars' worth of seedlings we have planted.
My colleague ought to acknowledge the boost our government has given to Canada's forest sector by establishing a full-fledged Department of Forestry. He should also admit-and it is unfortunate that he would not say so-that most cases related to public forests fall under provincial jurisdiction. This is something the federal government takes into account in all such agreements signed with British Columbia and Quebec. He cannot ignore the fact that it is the provinces' responsibility.
The Minister of Forestry said yes, we are prepared to work together. Yes we are prepared to renew the forest agreements inasmuch as each province demonstrates genuine interest in this natural resource. Mr. Speaker, that is our approach in the ongoing negotiations.
I would remind my colleague that the March 31 agreement has ended, It is true, there is a certain delay. But it is better to take the time required to sign an agreement that will benefit the provinces, the forestry industry and our young people's future than to sign an agreement prematurely to satisfy the very short-term needs of individuals who want to keep their original businesses running some way or other. The goal of the federal government and the Department of Forestry is to reach solid, lasting agreements for sustainable development in the interests of future generations. That is what we want, Mr. Speaker.

June 11, 1990
1990 CONSTITUTIONAL AGREEMENT
WHEREAS on April 30,1987, the Prime Minister of Canada and the Premiers reached agreement in principle on means to bring about the full and active participation of Quebec in Canada's constitutional evolution;
AND WHEREAS on June 3,1987, all first ministers signed the 1987 Constitutional Accord and committed themselves to introducing as soon as possible the Constitution Amendment, 1987 in Parliament and the provincial legislative assemblies;
AND WHEREAS the Constitution Amendment, 1987 has been authorized by Parliament and the legislative assemblies of Quebec, Saskatchewan, Alberta, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, Ontario and British Columbia:
1.	THE MEECH LAKE ACCORD
The Premiers of New Brunswick, Manitoba and Newfoundland undertake to submit the Constitution Amendment, 1987 for appropriate legislative or public consideration and to use every possible effort to achieve decision prior to June 23, 1990.
2.	SENATE REFORM
After proclamation, the federal government and the provinces will constitute a commission with equal representation for each province and an appropriate number of territorial and federal representatives to conduct hearings and to report to Parliament and the legislative assemblies oi the provinces and territories, prior to the First Ministers' conference on the Senate to be held by the end of 1990 in British Columbia, on specific proposals for Senate reform that will give effect to the following objectives:
-	The Senate should be elected.
-	The Senate should provide for more equitable representation of the less populous provinces and territories.
-	The Senate should have effective powers to ensure the interests of residents of the less populous provinces and territories figure more prominently in national decision-making, reflect Canadian duality and strengthen the Government of Canada's capacity to govern on behalf of all citizens, while preserving the principle of the responsibility of the Government to the House of Commons.
Following proclamation of the Meech Lake Accord, the Prime Minister and all Premiers agree to seek adoption of an amendment on comprehensive Senate reform consistent with these objectives by July 1, 1995.
The Prime Minister undertakes to report semi-annually to the House of Commons on progress achieved towards comprehensive Senate reform.
The Prime Minister and all Premiers, reaffirming the commitment made in the Edmonton Declaration and the provisions to be entrenched under the Constitution Amendment, 1987, undertook that Senate reform will be the key constitutional priority until comprehensive reform is achieved.
June 11, 1990

If, by July 1,1995, comprehensive Senate reform has not been achieved according to the objectives set out above under section 41 of the Constitution Act, 1982, as amended by the Constitution Amendment, 1987, the number of Senators by which a province is entitled to be represented in the Senate will be amended so that, of the total of one hundred and four Senators, the representation of Ontario will be eighteen Senators, the representation of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Newfounland will be eight Senators each, and the representation of all other provinces and the territories will remain unchanged. In the case of any province whose representation declined, no new appointments would be made until that province's representation had by attrition declined below its new maximum. In the event of such a redistribution of Senate seats, Newfoundland would be entitled to another Member of Parliament in the House of Commons under section 51A of the Constitution Act, 1867.
3.	FURTHER CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENTS
(1)	Charter-Sex Equality Rights
Add section 28 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedom to section 16 of the Constitution Amendment, 1987.
(2)	Role of the Territories
-	In appointments to the Senate and the Supreme Court of Canada.
In discussions on items on the agenda of annual constitutional and economic conferences where, in the view of the Prime Minister, matters to be discussed directly affect them.
(3)	Language Issues
-	Add to the agenda of constitutional conferences matters that are of interest to English-speaking and Frenchspeaking linguistic minorities.
Require resolutions of the House of Commons, the Senate and the legislative assembly of New Brunswick to amend that province's Act Recognizing the Equality of the Two Official Linguistic Communities in New Brunswick (Bill 88).
(4)	Aboriginal Constitutional	Issues
First Ministers' constitutional conferences to be held once every three years, the first to be held within one year of proclamation; representatives of aboriginal peoples and the territorial governments to be invited by the Prime Minister to participate in the discussion of matters of interest to the aboriginal peoples of Canada.
The Prime Minister of Canada will lay or cause to be laid before the Senate and House of Commons, and the Premiers will lay or cause to be laid before their legislative assemblies, a resolution, in the form appended hereto, and will seek to authorize a proclamation to be issued by the Governor General under the Great Seal of Canada to amend the constitution of Canada as soon as possible after proclamation of the Constitution Amendment, 1987.

June 11, 1990
4.	AGENDA FOR FUTURE CONSTITUTIONAL DISCUSSIONS
(1)	Creation of New Provinces in the Territories
The Prime Minister and all Premiers agreed future constitutional conferences should address available options for provincehood, including the possibility that, at the request of the Yukon and Northwest Territories to become provinces, only a resolution of the House of Commons and Senate be required.
(2)	Constitutional Recognitions
The Prime Minister and Premiers took note of repeated attempts by First Ministers over the past twenty years to draft a statement of constitutional recognitions. All such attempts were unsuccessful.
The Prime Minister and Premiers reviewed drafts submitted by the federal government and Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Ontario and British Columbia, and agreed to refer immediately the drafts to an all-party Special Committee of the House of Commons. Public hearings would begin across Canada on July 16,1990 and a report on the substance and placement of the clause-in a manner consistent with the Constitution of Canada-would be prepared for consideration by First Ministers at their Conference in 1990.
(3)	Constitutional Reviews
The Prime Minister and all Premiers agreed jointly to review, at the constitutional conference required by section 49 of the Constitution Act, 1982: the entire process of amending the Constitution, including the three-year time limit under section 39(2) of that Act and the question of mandatory public hearings prior to adopting any measure related to a constitutional amendment, including revocation of a constitutional resolution.
Pursuant to section 50 of the Constitution Act, 1982, as proposed in the Constitution Amendment, 1987, the Prime Minister and the Premiers also committed to a continuing review of the operation of the Constitution of Canada, including the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, with a view to making any appropriate constitutional amendments.
5.	SECTION 2: CONSTITUTION AMENDMENT, 1987
The Prime Minister and Premiers took note of public discussion of the distinct society clause since its inclusion in the Meech Lake Accord. A number of Canada's most distinguished constitutional authorities met to exchange views on the legal impact of the clause. The Prime Minister and Premiers reviewed their advice and other material.
The Prime Minister, in his capacity as chairman of the Conference, received from the above-noted constitutional authorities a legal opinion which is appended to the final Conference communique.
June 11, 1990

6.	NEW BRUNSWICK AMENDMENT
-	Add a clause that within New Brunswick, the English linguistic community and the French linguistic community have equality of status and equal rights and privileges.
Affirm an additional role of the legislature and government of New Brunswick: to preserve and promote the equality of status and equal rights and privileges of the province's two official linguistic communities.
The Prime Minister of Canada will lay or cause to be laid before the Senate and House of Commons, and the Premier of New Brunswick will lay or cause to be laid before the legislative assembly of New Brunswick, a resolution, in the form appended hereto, and will seek to authorize a proclamation to be issued by the Governor General under the Great Seal of Canada to amend the Constitution of Canada as soon as possible after proclamation of the Constitution Amendment, 1987.

OTTAWA June 9, 1990
Dear Prime Minister:
In response to certain concerns which have been expressed in relation to section I of the proposed Constitution Amendment, 1987 (Meech Lake Accord), it is our pleasure to confirm our opinion on the following.
In our opinion, the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms will be interpreted in a manner consistent with the duality/distinct society clause for the proposed Constitution Amendment, 1987 (Meech Lake Accord), but the rights and freedoms guaranteed thereunder are not infringed or denied by the application of the clause and continue to be guaranteed subject only to such reasonable limits prescribed by law as can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society, and the duality/distinct society clause may be considered, in particular, in the application of section I of the Charter.
The Constitution of Canada, including sections 91 and 92 of the Constitution Act, 1867, will be interpreted in a manner consistent with the duality/distinct society clause. While nothing in that clause creates new legislative authority for Parliament or any of the provincial legislatures, or derogates from any of their legislative authority, it may be considered in determining whether a particular law fits within the legislative authority of Parliament or any of the legislatures.
